questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The mobility of the free electrons in a metal is 4.0 × 10⁻³ m² V⁻¹ s⁻¹. Taking the electron mass as 9.0 × 10⁻³¹ kg and e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, the average relaxation time of the free electrons is:

solution.concept: Mobility μ = v_d/E = eτ/m, so τ = μm/e
solution.explanation: The drift speed acquired in a field E is eEτ/m, so the mobility (drift speed per unit field) is eτ/m. Solving for the relaxation time gives τ = μm/e.
solution.why_others_wrong: 7.1 × 10⁸ s comes from μe/m, the inverted relation (and its unit would be s⁻¹, not s). 1.1 × 10⁻¹⁴ s and 4.5 × 10⁻¹⁴ s bring in a spurious factor of 1/2 or 2 in the relation μ = eτ/m.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', drift of electrons and the origin of resistivity; mobility

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A metal tube 3.14 m long has an outer radius of 3 mm and an inner radius of 1 mm. The resistivity of the metal is 2.0 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m. Taking π = 3.14, the resistance of the tube between its two ends (current flowing along its length) is:

solution.concept: R = ρL/A, where A is the area of the conducting cross-section
solution.explanation: The current flows through the metal wall only, so the cross-sectional area is the ring between the two circles: A = π(r₂² − r₁²).
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.2 × 10⁻³ Ω uses the full disc of the outer radius, ignoring the hollow. 5.0 × 10⁻³ Ω uses π(r₂ − r₁)² instead of π(r₂² − r₁²). 2.0 × 10⁻² Ω uses the area of the inner circle, which carries no current.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', resistivity of various materials (R = ρl/A)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Three resistors of 2 Ω, 3 Ω and 6 Ω are available. The ratio of the largest to the smallest equivalent resistance that can be obtained by connecting all three of them together is:

solution.concept: Series gives the largest and parallel the smallest equivalent resistance
solution.explanation: With all three used, the largest resistance is the series value and the smallest is the parallel value, which is less than the smallest single resistor.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5.5 takes the smallest resistance as 2 Ω, the smallest single resistor, but a parallel combination is less than its smallest member. 6 takes the largest resistance as the largest single resistor. 1/11 inverts the ratio asked for.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', combination of resistors - series and parallel

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A cell of emf 1.5 V gives a current of 3.0 A when its terminals are joined by a thick wire of negligible resistance. When the same cell is connected across a 1.0 Ω resistor instead, the potential difference between its terminals is:

solution.concept: Short-circuit current ε/r gives the internal resistance; then V = ε − Ir
solution.explanation: On short circuit the whole emf drives current through the internal resistance alone: r = ε/I_sc. With the external resistor, I = ε/(R + r) and the terminal voltage is IR.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.5 V is the emf, the terminal voltage only when no current is drawn. 0.5 V is the drop inside the cell, not across its terminals. 3.0 V multiplies the short-circuit current by the external resistance, but that current no longer flows once the resistor is connected.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', cells, emf, internal resistance

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The dimensional formula of the electrical conductivity σ of a material (σ = 1/ρ, where ρ is its resistivity) is:

solution.concept: Dimensions from R = V/I and ρ = RA/L
solution.explanation: Resistance R = V/I has dimensions [M L² T⁻³ A⁻²]. Resistivity ρ = RA/L adds one power of length: [M L³ T⁻³ A⁻²]. Conductivity is its reciprocal.
steps: [V] = [M L² T⁻³ A⁻¹], so [R] = [M L² T⁻³ A⁻²]
solution.why_others_wrong: [M L³ T⁻³ A⁻²] is the resistivity itself. [M⁻¹ L⁻² T³ A²] is the conductance (1/R), which lacks the length factor. [M⁻¹ L⁻¹ T³ A²] has the wrong power of length.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', Ohm's law; resistivity and conductivity

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A charge of 120 C flows at a steady rate through a 5 Ω resistor in 1 minute. The heat produced in the resistor is:

solution.concept: Joule heating H = I²Rt with I = Q/t
solution.explanation: A steady flow of 120 C in 60 s is a current of 2 A. The heat produced is I²Rt (equivalently QV, with V = IR = 10 V).
solution.why_others_wrong: 72 kJ uses Q²R, which is not a heat (it leaves out the division by t). 20 J is I²R, the power in watts, not the heat in one minute. 600 J halves the correct value, as if the energy were ½QV (the energy stored in a capacitor), but a resistor carrying a steady current dissipates QV.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', electrical energy, power

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A uniform wire of resistance 36 Ω is bent into a complete circle. The resistance between two points on the circle whose radii make an angle of 60° with each other is:

solution.concept: The two arcs between the points are in parallel; arc resistance is proportional to arc length
solution.explanation: The 60° arc is 1/6 of the circle and the other arc is 5/6 of it. Current can go either way round, so the two arcs are in parallel.
steps: Short arc: 36/6 = 6 Ω; long arc: 36 × 5/6 = 30 Ω
solution.why_others_wrong: 6 Ω and 30 Ω are the two arcs taken alone; the other path is ignored. 9 Ω is the resistance between diametrically opposite points (two 18 Ω halves in parallel).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', combination of resistors

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The heating coil of a toaster has a resistance of 50 Ω at 20 °C. When it is connected to a 220 V supply, the current settles at a steady value of 4.0 A. The temperature coefficient of resistance of its alloy is 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ °C⁻¹ (constant, referred to 20 °C). The steady temperature of the coil is:

solution.concept: R_T = R₂₀[1 + α(T − 20 °C)]; the hot resistance is V/I
solution.explanation: At the steady temperature the coil's resistance is 220 V/4.0 A = 55 Ω. The fractional rise in resistance, divided by α, gives the rise in temperature above 20 °C.
solution.why_others_wrong: 500 °C is only the rise in temperature; the coil started at 20 °C. 'About 475 °C' divides the change in resistance by the hot resistance (55 Ω) instead of the resistance at the reference temperature. 5520 °C uses R_T/R₂₀ in place of (R_T/R₂₀ − 1).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', temperature dependence of resistivity

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A cell of emf ε and internal resistance r is connected across an external resistor R. The power delivered to the resistor when R = 2r, expressed as a fraction of the largest power the cell can deliver to any external resistor, is:

solution.concept: Power in the load P = ε²R/(R + r)²; it is greatest when R = r, where P_max = ε²/(4r)
solution.explanation: Write the load power for R = 2r and divide by the maximum value, which occurs at R = r.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2/3 is the efficiency R/(R + r) at R = 2r, the fraction of the cell's own output delivered to the load, not a comparison with the maximum. 1/2 is the efficiency at maximum power. 4/9 is (2/3)², a wrong way of scaling the power.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', cells, emf, internal resistance; electrical power

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In a metre bridge, an ideal cell of emf 2.0 V is connected directly across the two ends of the 100 cm bridge wire, whose resistance is 4.0 Ω. An unknown resistance X is in the left gap and a known resistance in the right gap, and the null point is found 40.0 cm from the left end. At balance, the potential difference across X is:

solution.concept: At the null point the jockey and the X-R junction are at the same potential
solution.explanation: The cell maintains 2.0 V across the uniform wire, so the potential falls uniformly along it. The gap resistances X and R are connected between the same two ends as the wire. At balance the junction of X and R is at the same potential as the null point, so the drop across X equals the drop across the first 40.0 cm of wire.
steps: Potential drop per cm of wire = 2.0 V/100 cm = 0.020 V/cm
So the potential difference across X = 0.80 V (and across R it is 1.20 V)
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.20 V is the drop across the right-hand 60 cm, i.e. across the known resistance. 2.0 V is the whole emf, shared between X and the known resistance. 1.6 V multiplies the wire's 4.0 Ω by 0.4 as if it were a current in amperes.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', Wheatstone bridge; metre bridge (balance condition)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: While solving a circuit with Kirchhoff's rules, a student assumes that the current in one branch flows from point P to point Q, and the equations give this current as −2 A. This result means that:

options.text: the equations are inconsistent, so the circuit must be solved again with the opposite direction assumed
a current of 2 A flows from P to Q, the negative sign showing only that the branch contains a cell
a current of 2 A flows in that branch from Q to P
no current flows in that branch, because a current cannot be negative

solution.concept: Assumed directions of currents in Kirchhoff's rules
solution.explanation: The direction of each unknown current may be assumed arbitrarily. If the solution comes out negative, the magnitude is still correct and the actual current flows opposite to the assumed direction; nothing needs to be solved again.
steps: Magnitude 2 A, actual direction Q → P
solution.why_others_wrong: The equations are consistent; a negative value is a normal outcome of an arbitrary choice of direction. The sign has nothing to do with whether the branch contains a cell. A negative current is a current in the opposite direction, not zero.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', Kirchhoff's rules
solution.final_answer: Option C: a current of 2 A flows in that branch from Q to P

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Two cells of emfs ε₁ and ε₂ (ε₁ > ε₂) and internal resistances r₁ and r₂ are connected in series, with the negative terminal of one joined to the negative terminal of the other. The internal resistance of the combination is r₁ + r₂.
Statement II: For the same connection, the emf of the combination is ε₁ − ε₂.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Cells in series: emfs add algebraically, internal resistances always add
solution.explanation: Whichever way round the cells are joined, the current passes through both internal resistances one after the other, so r_eq = r₁ + r₂ (Statement I true). When like terminals are joined, the emfs act against each other and the net emf is ε₁ − ε₂ (Statement II true).
steps: Statement I: series internal resistances add → true
Statement II: opposing emfs subtract → true
solution.why_others_wrong: Reversing a cell changes the sign of its emf in the sum but not its internal resistance, so neither statement is false.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', cells in series and in parallel
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): For a metal wire carrying a large current, the graph of the potential difference V across it (y-axis) against the current I (x-axis) bends upwards, its slope increasing as the current increases.
Reason (R): A large current heats the wire, and the resistivity of a metal increases as its temperature rises.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Ohm's law holds only at constant temperature; resistivity of metals rises with temperature
solution.explanation: The slope V/I of the graph is the resistance. A large current raises the temperature of the wire (Joule heating), the resistivity of the metal increases, and so the resistance, and with it the slope, increases. R is therefore the direct cause of A.
steps: A: true (V–I graph curves away from the straight line)
R: true (ρ of a metal increases with T)
Rising resistance with heating is exactly why the slope increases → R explains A
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true and the heating of the wire is the cause of the departure from the straight line, so the options saying R does not explain A, or that either statement is false, are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', limitations of Ohm's law; temperature dependence of resistivity
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A battery of emf 12 V and internal resistance 2 Ω is connected, in turn, to each external resistor listed in List-I. Match each resistor with the power dissipated in it (List-II).

List-I:
A. 2 Ω
B. 4 Ω
C. 10 Ω
D. 22 Ω

List-II:
I. 10 W
II. 18 W
III. 5.5 W
IV. 16 W

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Power in the load P = I²R with I = ε/(R + r)
solution.explanation: For each resistor find I = 12/(R + 2) and then P = I²R. The power is greatest (18 W) when R equals the internal resistance.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes exchange 18 W and 16 W (forgetting that maximum power occurs at R = r) or 10 W and 5.5 W (as if power always rose with R).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', cells, emf, internal resistance; electrical power
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In a Wheatstone bridge, P = 2 Ω joins A to B, Q = 4 Ω joins B to C, R = 4 Ω joins A to D and S = 2 Ω joins D to C. An ideal 6 V battery is connected with its positive terminal at A and its negative terminal at C, and a galvanometer of resistance 4 Ω is connected between B and D. The current through the galvanometer is:

options.text: zero, because the bridge is balanced

solution.concept: Kirchhoff's junction rule at B and D (node potentials), with the galvanometer treated as a 4 Ω resistor
solution.explanation: P/Q = 1/2 but R/S = 2, so the bridge is not balanced. Take C as 0 V and A as 6 V and write the junction rule at B and at D, including the current through the galvanometer.
steps: I_G = (3.6 − 2.4)/4 = 0.30 A, from B (higher potential) to D
solution.why_others_wrong: 'From D to B' reverses the direction: B is at the higher potential. 0.75 A is the galvanometer current if its resistance is ignored (B and D at the same potential). The bridge is not balanced, because P/Q ≠ R/S.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', Kirchhoff's rules; Wheatstone bridge
solution.final_answer: Option D: 0.30 A, from B to D

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A wire-frame cube is built from twelve equal resistors of 4.0 Ω, one along each edge. A battery is connected between two corners A and C that lie diagonally opposite each other on one face (they are not joined by an edge and are not the ends of a body diagonal). The equivalent resistance of the frame between A and C is:

solution.concept: Symmetry of the network and Kirchhoff's junction rule
solution.explanation: Hold A at potential V and C at zero. Let B and D be the other two corners of the face ABCD, and A', B', C', D' the corners of the opposite face directly behind A, B, C, D. The mirror plane that swaps A and C (and V with 0) maps B, D, B' and D' onto themselves, so these four corners are all at V/2. Let A' be at potential x; then C' is at V − x. The junction rule at A' fixes x, and the current leaving A then gives the resistance.
steps: Junction rule at A' (edge resistance r): (V − x) + 2(V/2 − x) = 0 → x = 2V/3
Current leaving A: to B and D, 2 × (V/2)/r = V/r; to A', (V − 2V/3)/r = V/(3r)
solution.shortcut: For a cube of edge resistance r: adjacent corners 7r/12, face diagonal 3r/4, body diagonal 5r/6.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.3 Ω (7r/12) is the resistance between the ends of one edge, and 3.3 Ω (5r/6) is between the ends of a body diagonal. 4.0 Ω (= r) keeps only the two two-edge paths round the face, in parallel, and ignores the rest of the cube.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', combination of resistors; Kirchhoff's rules

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Three branches are connected in parallel between two points P and Q. Branch 1 is a cell of emf 6 V and internal resistance 1 Ω; branch 2 is a cell of emf 3 V and internal resistance 1 Ω; branch 3 is a 2 Ω resistor. Both cells have their positive terminals towards P. The current in the 2 Ω resistor, and the current in the 3 V cell, are:

options.text: 1.8 A; 0.6 A, leaving the positive terminal of the 3 V cell
2.0 A; zero in the 3 V cell
1.8 A; 0.6 A, entering the positive terminal of the 3 V cell
3.0 A; 3.0 A, leaving the positive terminal of the 3 V cell

solution.concept: Kirchhoff's junction rule at P with V = V_P − V_Q as the unknown
solution.explanation: Let V be the potential of P above Q. The current leaving P through each cell branch is (V − ε)/r, and through the resistor it is V/2. Their sum must be zero.
steps: Current in the 2 Ω resistor = 3.6/2 = 1.8 A
3 V cell: (3.6 − 3)/1 = 0.6 A flows from P into its positive terminal, so it is being charged
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Leaving the positive terminal' would mean the 3 V cell is discharging, but V_PQ = 3.6 V exceeds its emf, so it is being charged. '2.0 A; zero' ignores the 3 V cell and uses only the 6 V cell. '3.0 A' wrongly puts the two cells in series round one loop with the resistor.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', Kirchhoff's rules
solution.final_answer: Option C: 1.8 A; 0.6 A, entering the positive terminal of the 3 V cell

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Three identical bulbs A, B and C are connected to an ideal battery: B and C are in parallel with each other, and this pair is in series with A. Treat the resistance of each bulb as constant. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) Bulb A glows the brightest of the three.
(b) Each of B and C dissipates one-quarter of the power dissipated in A.
(c) If the filament of C breaks, A becomes dimmer and B becomes brighter.
(d) If B is short-circuited by a wire of negligible resistance, C goes out and A becomes brighter.
(e) If the filament of C breaks, the total power drawn from the battery increases.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Series-parallel combination; P = I²R for equal resistances
solution.explanation: Let each bulb have resistance R and the battery voltage be V. Initially R_eq = 1.5R, so the current through A is I = V/(1.5R) and B and C carry I/2 each. A dissipates I²R and each of B, C dissipates (I/2)²R = I²R/4, so (a) and (b) are true. If C breaks, A and B are in series: the current V/(2R) is less than I, so A is dimmer, but B now carries V/(2R), more than I/2, so B is brighter (c true). Shorting B also shorts C (they are in parallel), and A gets the full battery voltage, so it becomes brighter (d true). When C breaks, R_eq rises from 1.5R to 2R, so the total power V²/R_eq decreases (e false).
steps: (a) P_A = I²R is the largest → true
(c) I_A: V/1.5R → V/2R (dimmer); I_B: V/3R → V/2R (brighter) → true
(d) A gets full V, power V²/R > (4/9)V²/R → true
(e) R_eq increases, so total power decreases → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Options without (d) miss that shorting B also removes C from the circuit and puts the full voltage across A. Options with (e) forget that removing a parallel path increases the equivalent resistance and so reduces the total power.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', combination of resistors; electrical power

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A metal wire is connected across an ideal battery that keeps a fixed potential difference between its ends. The wire is then heated to a higher temperature, its dimensions remaining practically unchanged. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) The average relaxation time of the free electrons decreases.
(b) The resistivity of the metal increases.
(c) The drift speed of the free electrons decreases.
(d) The electric field inside the wire decreases.
(e) The power dissipated in the wire decreases.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: ρ = m/(ne²τ); v_d = eEτ/m; E = V/L; P = V²/R
solution.explanation: At a higher temperature the ions vibrate more and the electrons collide more often, so τ decreases (a true) and ρ = m/(ne²τ) increases (b true); n hardly changes in a metal. The field E = V/L is fixed by the battery and the length (d false), so the drift speed eEτ/m decreases with τ (c true). The resistance rises, so the power V²/R falls (e true).
steps: (c) v_d = eEτ/m with E fixed → decreases → true
solution.why_others_wrong: Options containing (d) wrongly let the field change; it is fixed by the battery voltage and the length. The option without (b) misses the basic increase of resistivity with temperature.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', drift of electrons and the origin of resistivity; temperature dependence of resistivity

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): In a Wheatstone bridge in which P/Q = R/S, the current in the galvanometer arm stays zero even if the galvanometer is replaced by a resistor of any value.
Reason (R): When P/Q = R/S, the two ends of the galvanometer arm are at the same potential, so no current flows through a resistor of any value connected between them.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Balance condition of the Wheatstone bridge
solution.explanation: With P/Q = R/S, the potential at the P-Q junction equals that at the R-S junction (each branch divides the battery voltage in the same ratio). A resistor (or galvanometer) joining two points at equal potential carries no current, whatever its resistance, and with no current in it the potentials stay equal. So the reason given is exactly why the assertion holds.
steps: Potentials: V_B = V_D when P/Q = R/S
ΔV = 0 across the arm → I = 0 for any resistance
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true and the equality of potentials is the cause of zero current in the arm, so the options saying R is not the explanation, or that either statement is false, are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', Wheatstone bridge
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A rectangular coil of 50 turns, each measuring 5.0 cm × 8.0 cm, carries a current of 2.0 A. It is placed in a uniform magnetic field of 0.50 T so that the normal to the plane of the coil makes an angle of 30° with the field. The magnitude of the torque on the coil is:

solution.concept: Torque on a current loop τ = NIAB sin θ, θ being the angle between the normal (magnetic moment) and B
solution.explanation: The magnetic moment of the coil is NIA along its normal, and the torque is m × B, of magnitude NIAB sin θ with θ = 30°.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.17 N m uses cos 30°, which is correct only if 30° is the angle between the plane of the coil and the field. 0.20 N m is the maximum torque (sin θ = 1). 2.0 × 10⁻³ N m leaves out the 50 turns.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', torque on current loop, magnetic dipole

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A long solenoid is made by winding a single layer of insulated wire of diameter 0.50 mm on a long tube, with the turns touching one another. A current of 2.0 A flows through it. Taking μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹, the magnetic field well inside the solenoid is about:

solution.concept: B = μ₀nI for a long solenoid; for close-wound turns n = 1/(wire diameter)
solution.explanation: With the turns touching, each turn occupies a length equal to the wire diameter, so the number of turns per metre is 1/(0.50 × 10⁻³ m) = 2000 m⁻¹.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.5 × 10⁻³ T takes 1000 turns per metre (treating 0.50 mm as the radius and doubling it). 1.0 × 10⁻² T takes 4000 turns per metre. 8.0 × 10⁻⁴ T divides by 2π as in the field of a straight wire.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', the solenoid

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: When a superconducting material is cooled below its transition temperature in a magnetic field, the field lines are completely expelled from its interior and it behaves as a perfect diamagnet (χ = −1). This phenomenon is known as:

solution.concept: Perfect diamagnetism of superconductors
solution.explanation: NCERT notes that the most exotic diamagnetic materials are superconductors, metals cooled to very low temperatures, which show perfect conductivity and perfect diamagnetism. The complete expulsion of the magnetic field from a superconductor is called the Meissner effect.
steps: Name of the phenomenon: Meissner effect
solution.why_others_wrong: Hysteresis is the lag of magnetisation behind the applied field in ferromagnets. The Curie point is the temperature at which a ferromagnet becomes paramagnetic. Electromagnetic induction is the production of emf by a changing magnetic flux.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Magnetism and Matter', magnetic properties of materials - diamagnetism

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A long solenoid with 1000 turns per metre carries a current of 2.0 A. Its core is filled with a material of magnetic susceptibility 3.0 × 10⁻⁴. The magnetisation of the core is:

solution.concept: Magnetic intensity H = nI; magnetisation M = χH
solution.explanation: Inside a long solenoid the magnetic intensity is H = nI, set by the winding alone. The magnetisation produced in a linear material is M = χH.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.0 × 10³ A m⁻¹ is H, not M. 6.7 × 10⁶ A m⁻¹ divides H by χ instead of multiplying. 7.5 × 10⁻⁷ is μ₀M, which is in tesla (the extra field due to the core), not the magnetisation.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Magnetism and Matter', magnetisation and magnetic intensity

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: An ammeter is connected in series with the part of a circuit whose current is to be measured, and a voltmeter is connected in parallel with the element across which the potential difference is to be measured.
Statement II: An ideal voltmeter has zero resistance.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Use of ammeters and voltmeters made from galvanometers
solution.explanation: An ammeter must carry the current being measured, so it goes in series; a voltmeter must have the same potential difference as the element, so it goes in parallel (Statement I true). A voltmeter should draw as little current as possible, so an ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance, not zero (Statement II false).
steps: Statement II: ideal voltmeter → infinite resistance → false
solution.why_others_wrong: A zero-resistance voltmeter in parallel would short-circuit the element, so Statement II cannot be true.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', moving coil galvanometer (conversion into ammeter and voltmeter)
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A 2.0 Ω resistor is connected across an ideal 6.0 V battery. An ammeter of resistance 0.50 Ω is then connected in series with the resistor to measure the current. The reading of the ammeter is:

solution.concept: A real ammeter adds its own resistance in series and so reduces the current it measures
solution.explanation: Once the ammeter is in the circuit, the battery drives current through the resistor and the ammeter in series, so the current is 6.0/(2.0 + 0.50) A. This is less than the 3.0 A that flowed without the ammeter; that is why a good ammeter must have a very small resistance.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3.0 A is the current before the ammeter was inserted. 12 A divides the emf by the ammeter's resistance alone. 0.60 A is the drop in current caused by the ammeter, not its reading.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', moving coil galvanometer (ammeter)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A toroid is wound uniformly on a ring-shaped core whose inner radius is 10 cm and outer radius is 15 cm. A steady current flows in the winding. Within the core, the ratio of the magnetic field at the inner edge (r = 10 cm) to that at the outer edge (r = 15 cm) is:

solution.concept: Ampere's law for a toroid: B × 2πr = μ₀NI, so B = μ₀NI/(2πr) inside the core
solution.explanation: A circular Amperian loop of radius r inside the core is threaded by all N turns, each carrying I. B is constant along the loop by symmetry, so B = μ₀NI/(2πr): the field varies inversely as r across the core.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.25 uses B ∝ 1/r². 0.67 inverts the ratio. 1 assumes the field is the same everywhere in the core, which holds only when the core is thin compared with its radius (the usual approximation B = μ₀nI).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', Ampere's circuital law; the toroid

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A metal rod of mass 0.20 kg rests at right angles across two horizontal parallel rails 0.50 m apart. The coefficient of static friction between the rod and the rails is 0.25. A uniform vertical magnetic field of 0.50 T acts in the region. Taking g = 10 m/s², the least current that must be passed through the rod (via the rails) to make it just start sliding is:

solution.concept: Force on a current-carrying conductor F = BIL; limiting static friction μmg
solution.explanation: The vertical field and the horizontal rod are perpendicular, so the magnetic force BIL is horizontal, along the rails. The rod starts to slide when this force equals the limiting friction μN = μmg.
solution.why_others_wrong: 8.0 A balances the weight mg instead of the friction μmg. 0.50 A is the friction force (in newtons) reported as a current. 10 A leaves the mass out of the friction force.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', magnetic force on a current-carrying conductor

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: Two long straight parallel wires, 6.0 cm apart, carry steady currents of 10 A each in opposite directions. Point P lies on the perpendicular bisector of the line joining the wires, in the plane perpendicular to them, at a distance of 4.0 cm from the midpoint of that line (so P is 5.0 cm from each wire). Taking μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹, the magnitude of the resultant magnetic field at P is:

solution.concept: Field of a long straight wire B = μ₀I/(2πr), perpendicular to the radius; vector addition
solution.explanation: Each wire produces B = μ₀I/(2πr) = 4.0 × 10⁻⁵ T at P, perpendicular to the line from that wire to P. With the currents opposite, the components parallel to the line joining the wires cancel and the components along the bisector add. Each field makes an angle θ with the bisector direction where cos θ = 3/5.
solution.why_others_wrong: 6.4 × 10⁻⁵ T (= 2B × 4/5) is the result for currents in the same direction. 8.0 × 10⁻⁵ T adds the two fields as if they were parallel. Zero would hold only for same-direction currents at the midpoint, not here.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', magnetic field due to a straight current-carrying wire

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: Two identical short bar magnets, each of magnetic moment m, are fixed with their centres at the same point and their axes at right angles to each other, forming a cross. The pair is equivalent to a single magnetic dipole of moment:

options.text: √2 m, directed at 45° to the axis of each magnet
2m, directed along the bisector of the angle between their axes
m, directed along the axis of either magnet

solution.concept: Magnetic dipole moment is a vector; moments add vectorially
solution.explanation: The two moments have equal magnitude m and are perpendicular, so their vector sum has magnitude √(m² + m²) = √2 m and lies along the bisector, at 45° to each.
steps: Direction: along the bisector, 45° to each axis
solution.why_others_wrong: 2m adds the magnitudes as if the moments were parallel. Zero would need antiparallel moments. m ignores one of the two magnets.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Magnetism and Matter', the bar magnet (magnetic dipole moment)
solution.final_answer: Option A: √2 m, directed at 45° to the axis of each magnet

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): To convert a given galvanometer into an ammeter of a larger range, a shunt of smaller resistance is needed.
Reason (R): The shunt is connected in series with the galvanometer so that it takes most of the potential difference.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Conversion of a galvanometer into an ammeter: shunt in parallel, I_g G = (I − I_g) S
solution.explanation: The shunt S is connected in parallel with the galvanometer, so that most of the current bypasses it. From I_g G = (I − I_g)S, S = I_g G/(I − I_g): a larger range I needs a smaller S. So A is true. R is false: a resistance in series with the galvanometer, taking most of the voltage, is how a voltmeter is made.
steps: A: S = I_g G/(I − I_g) decreases as I increases → true
R: the shunt is in parallel, not in series → false
solution.why_others_wrong: R describes the conversion into a voltmeter, so it is false here; options that treat R as true are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', moving coil galvanometer
solution.final_answer: Option C: A is true but R is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: A proton and an electron move at right angles to the same uniform magnetic field with momenta of equal magnitude. They take equal times to complete one revolution.
Statement II: In this situation, the radii of their circular paths are equal.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Circular motion in a magnetic field: r = mv/(qB) = p/(qB), T = 2πm/(qB)
solution.explanation: The radius r = p/(qB) depends only on the momentum and the charge, and the charges have equal magnitude, so equal momenta give equal radii (Statement II true). The period 2πm/(qB) depends on the mass; the electron is about 1836 times lighter and goes round much faster (Statement I false).
steps: r = p/(|q|B): equal p, equal |q| → equal r → II true
T = 2πm/(|q|B): different m → different T → I false
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement I would be true only for particles of equal mass-to-charge ratio, which a proton and an electron are not.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', motion in a magnetic field
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
Each coil in List-I carries a current of 2.0 A. Match each coil with the magnitude of its magnetic dipole moment in List-II.

List-I:
A. A single circular turn of radius 10 cm
B. A square coil of 5 turns, side 10 cm
C. A rectangular coil of 10 turns, 5.0 cm × 20 cm
D. A circular coil of 50 turns, radius 2.0 cm

List-II:
I. 0.20 A m²
II. 0.063 A m²
III. 0.13 A m²
IV. 0.10 A m²

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Magnetic moment of a coil m = NIA
solution.explanation: Multiply the number of turns, the current and the area of one turn in each case.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes exchange the moments of coils A and B, or of C and D: the square coil has five turns, and the small circular coil gains from its 50 turns.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', the magnetic dipole moment of a current loop
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
Match each physical quantity in List-I with its SI unit expressed in SI base units (List-II).

List-I:
A. Magnetic field B
B. Magnetic flux
C. Permeability of free space μ₀
D. Magnetic dipole moment

List-II:
I. kg m² s⁻² A⁻¹
II. A m²
III. kg s⁻² A⁻¹
IV. kg m s⁻² A⁻²

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: F = qvB (or F = BIl) defines the tesla; Φ = BA; B = μ₀I/(2πr); m = IA
solution.explanation: From F = BIl, 1 T = 1 N A⁻¹ m⁻¹ = kg s⁻² A⁻¹. Flux adds m²: kg m² s⁻² A⁻¹. From B = μ₀I/(2πr), μ₀ has the unit T m A⁻¹ = kg m s⁻² A⁻². The magnetic moment IA is A m².
steps: B: N/(A m) = kg m s⁻²/(A m) = kg s⁻² A⁻¹
Φ: T m² = kg m² s⁻² A⁻¹
μ₀: T m A⁻¹ = kg m s⁻² A⁻²
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes exchange the field and the flux (which differ by m²), or the permeability and the dipole moment.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', magnetic force (unit of B); magnetic field due to a current element
solution.final_answer: Option A: A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A uniform magnetic field of 0.50 T fills the whole region on one side of a plane boundary and is parallel to that boundary. A proton (mass 1.6 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, charge 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) moving at 2.0 × 10⁶ m/s, perpendicular to the field, enters the field region with its velocity making an angle of 30° with the boundary. It moves along an arc and comes out again through the same boundary. The distance between the point where it enters and the point where it leaves is:

solution.concept: Circular motion r = mv/(qB); geometry of a chord: the angle between the tangent and the chord is half the arc
solution.explanation: Inside the field the proton moves on a circle of radius r = mv/(qB). The entry and exit points lie on the boundary, so they are the ends of a chord. The velocity (tangent) at entry makes 30° with this chord, so the chord length is 2r sin 30°, whichever way the proton curves.
solution.why_others_wrong: 6.9 cm uses 2r cos 30°, measuring the angle from the normal instead of from the boundary. 8.0 cm (= 2r) is the result for entry perpendicular to the boundary. 2.0 cm is r sin 30°, half the chord.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', motion in a magnetic field

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A horizontal metal rod 0.50 m long hangs from two identical light vertical springs, each of spring constant 10 N/m, attached at its ends, in a uniform horizontal magnetic field of 0.40 T perpendicular to the rod. With no current in the rod, each spring is stretched by 2.0 cm. When a current is passed through the rod, each spring is stretched by 3.0 cm. The current in the rod is:

solution.concept: Force on a conductor F = BIL, added to the weight; two springs share the load
solution.explanation: Without current the two springs together balance the weight: 2k × 0.020 m = 0.40 N. With the current, the magnetic force BIL acts downward and the extra extension of 1.0 cm in each spring supplies the extra force.
steps: (The current flows in the direction for which BIL points downwards.)
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.50 A uses only one spring. 3.0 A equates BIL to the whole spring force at 3.0 cm, which also includes the weight. 2.0 A equates BIL to the weight of the rod.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', magnetic force on a current-carrying conductor

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
A proton (mass 1.6 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, charge 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) enters a uniform magnetic field of 0.50 T with a speed of 2.0 × 10⁶ m/s, its velocity making an angle of 30° with the field. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) The radius of its helical path is 2.0 cm.
(b) It takes 4π × 10⁻⁸ s (about 1.26 × 10⁻⁷ s) to complete one turn of the helix.
(c) The pitch of the helix is about 12.6 cm.
(d) Its kinetic energy remains constant.
(e) The component of its velocity along the field stays equal to about 1.73 × 10⁶ m/s.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Helical motion: r = mv sin θ/(qB), T = 2πm/(qB), pitch = v cos θ × T
solution.explanation: Resolve the velocity into v cos θ along B (unaffected by the field) and v sin θ perpendicular to B (circular motion). r = m v sin θ/(qB) = 2.0 cm (a true). T = 2πm/(qB) = 4π × 10⁻⁸ s (b true). The pitch is the distance moved along B in one period: v cos θ × T ≈ 21.8 cm, not 12.6 cm (c false). The magnetic force does no work, so the kinetic energy is constant (d true), and v cos 30° ≈ 1.73 × 10⁶ m/s stays constant (e true).
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (c) use the perpendicular component v sin θ to find the pitch; the pitch depends on the component along the field. Options leaving out (b) or (e) miss correct statements.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', motion in a magnetic field (helical motion)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): At every point outside a long straight wire of circular cross-section, carrying a steady current spread uniformly over its cross-section, the magnetic field is the same as it would be if the whole current flowed along the axis of the wire.
Reason (R): A circular Amperian loop of radius r larger than the radius of the wire, coaxial with it, encloses the whole current I, and by symmetry the field is tangential to the loop with the same magnitude all round it, so B = μ₀I/(2πr).

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Ampere's circuital law applied to a cylindrically symmetric current
solution.explanation: For r outside the wire, ∮B·dl = B × 2πr and the enclosed current is the whole of I, so B = μ₀I/(2πr), exactly the field of a thin wire carrying I along the axis. The reason gives precisely this argument, so it explains the assertion.
steps: Same as a line current on the axis → A true; R true and explains A
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true and R is the derivation of A, so the options saying R does not explain A, or that either statement is false, are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', Ampere's circuital law (field of a long straight wire)
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: Two identical short bar magnets, each of magnetic moment 1.0 A m², lie along the same straight line with their centres 20 cm apart. Both magnetic moments point in the same direction along the line (the north pole of one faces the south pole of the other). Taking μ₀/4π = 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹ and ignoring all other magnetic fields, the magnitude of the magnetic field at the point midway between their centres is:

solution.concept: Axial field of a short magnet B = (μ₀/4π)(2m/r³), directed along m on both sides of the magnet
solution.explanation: The midpoint is on the axis of each magnet, 10 cm from each. On the axis of a short dipole the field points along its moment whichever side of the magnet the point lies, so both fields point the same way and add.
steps: Both along the common direction of the moments
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ T counts only one magnet. 'Zero' assumes that fields on opposite sides of the point cancel, but on the axis each field points along its own moment. 5.0 × 10⁻⁵ T uses the 20 cm separation instead of the 10 cm distance from each centre.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Magnetism and Matter', the bar magnet (field on the axis of a magnetic dipole)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: In the Bohr model of the hydrogen atom, the electron (charge 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) moves round the nucleus in a circle of radius 0.53 × 10⁻¹⁰ m with a speed of 2.2 × 10⁶ m/s. Treating the revolving electron as a circular current loop and taking μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹, the magnetic field it produces at the nucleus is about:

solution.concept: Equivalent current I = e/T = ev/(2πr); field at the centre of a loop B = μ₀I/(2r)
solution.explanation: The electron passes any point of its orbit once per period T = 2πr/v, so the equivalent current is I = ev/(2πr). The nucleus is at the centre of this current loop.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4.0 T uses μ₀I/(2πr), the field of a long straight wire. 79 T takes the current as ev/r, leaving out the 2π in the period. 6.3 T uses μ₀I/(4r), half the field at the centre of a full loop.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', magnetic field on the axis of a circular current loop (field at the centre)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In a region of space, the magnetic field has a magnitude of 0.20 T. Taking μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹, the magnetic energy stored per unit volume of this region is about:

solution.concept: Magnetic energy density u_B = B²/(2μ₀)
solution.explanation: NCERT obtains the energy stored in a solenoid as (1/2)LI² and rewrites it as B²/(2μ₀) per unit volume, a result that holds for any region of magnetic field in vacuum.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3.2 × 10⁴ J m⁻³ leaves out the factor 1/2. 8.0 × 10⁴ J m⁻³ uses B instead of B². 2.5 × 10⁻⁸ J m⁻³ multiplies by μ₀ instead of dividing.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', self-inductance (magnetic energy density B²/2μ₀)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An ideal step-down transformer is connected to the 220 V AC mains. Its secondary supplies 11 V to ten identical lamps connected in parallel, each rated 11 V, 22 W, all glowing normally. The current drawn from the mains by the primary is:

solution.concept: Ideal transformer: input power = output power, V_p I_p = V_s I_s
solution.explanation: The ten lamps together take 10 × 22 = 220 W from the secondary. An ideal transformer has no losses, so the primary draws the same 220 W from the 220 V mains.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 A is the secondary current. 0.10 A is the primary current for a single lamp. 400 A steps the current up by the turns ratio instead of down; in a step-down transformer the primary current is the smaller one.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Alternating Current', transformers

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A straight metal rod 0.50 m long moves in a plane perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 0.50 T. Its velocity, of magnitude 4.0 m/s, makes an angle of 30° with the length of the rod. The emf induced between the ends of the rod is:

solution.concept: Motional emf = B l v⊥, where v⊥ is the component of velocity perpendicular to the rod (and to B)
solution.explanation: Only the velocity component perpendicular to the rod sweeps out area (cuts field lines); motion along the rod's own length produces no emf. That component is v sin 30°.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.87 V uses the component along the rod (v cos 30°), which produces no emf. 1.0 V treats the motion as perpendicular to the rod. 0.25 V halves the correct value without reason.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', motional electromotive force

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: At resonance, the impedance of a series LCR circuit is equal to its resistance R.
Statement II: At resonance, the current in a series LCR circuit is in phase with the applied voltage.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Series resonance: X_L = X_C
solution.explanation: At resonance X_L = X_C, so Z = √(R² + (X_L − X_C)²) = R (Statement I true) and tan φ = (X_C − X_L)/R = 0, so the current and the voltage are in phase (Statement II true).
solution.why_others_wrong: Both follow from X_L = X_C, so no option with a false statement is right.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Alternating Current', series LCR circuit; resonance
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An AC voltmeter connected across the household mains reads 220 V. This reading is the:

options.text: peak value of the alternating voltage
average value of the voltage over a complete cycle
peak-to-peak value of the alternating voltage
rms value of the alternating voltage

solution.concept: AC meters are calibrated to read rms values
solution.explanation: NCERT notes that AC ammeters and voltmeters measure rms values, and that the household line voltage of 220 V is an rms value; the peak value is √2 × 220 ≈ 311 V.
solution.why_others_wrong: The peak value of the mains is about 311 V, not 220 V. The average of a sinusoidal voltage over a complete cycle is zero. The peak-to-peak value is about 622 V.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Alternating Current', AC voltage applied to a resistor (rms values)
solution.final_answer: Option D: rms value of the alternating voltage

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A coil of 50 turns, each of area 0.010 m², is held with its plane perpendicular to a magnetic field that varies with time as B = 0.20 sin(100πt) tesla, t being in seconds. The peak value of the emf induced in the coil is about:

solution.concept: Faraday's law ε = −N dΦ/dt with Φ = BA
solution.explanation: The flux through each turn is Φ = AB₀ sin ωt, so ε = −NAB₀ω cos ωt, whose peak value is NAB₀ω with ω = 100π rad/s.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.10 V is the peak flux linkage NAB₀ (in Wb), not an emf. 0.63 V leaves out the 50 turns. 10 V drops the factor π from ω = 100π.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', Faraday's law of induction

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An AC circuit connected to a 250 V (rms) supply draws an average power of 1.0 kW at a power factor of 0.80. The rms current in the circuit and the resistance of the circuit are:

solution.concept: Average power P = V_rms I_rms cos φ; the power is dissipated only in the resistance, P = I²_rms R
solution.explanation: Use P = VI cos φ to find the current, then P = I²R for the resistance (only the resistance absorbs average power).
solution.why_others_wrong: 4.0 A and 62.5 Ω ignore the power factor. 5.0 A and 50 Ω give the impedance V/I instead of the resistance. 6.25 A and 25.6 Ω divide by the power factor twice.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Alternating Current', power in AC circuit: the power factor

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A tuning circuit consists of a coil of inductance 1.0 mH in series with a variable capacitor. To make the circuit resonate at a frequency of 1.0 MHz, the capacitance must be set to (take π² = 10):

solution.concept: Resonant frequency f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)), so C = 1/(4π²f₀²L)
solution.explanation: Square the resonance condition and solve for C.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.0 nF leaves out the factor 4π². 159 pF uses 2π in place of 4π². 250 pF drops the π² (takes it as 1).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Alternating Current', series LCR circuit; resonance

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A long solenoid 20 cm long has 200 turns, each of cross-sectional area 1.0 cm². Its core is filled with a material of relative permeability 100 (take it as constant). Taking μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹, the self-inductance of the solenoid is about:

solution.concept: Self-inductance of a long solenoid with a core L = μᵣμ₀N²A/l
solution.explanation: The flux linkage per unit current of a long solenoid is μ₀n²Al = μ₀N²A/l in vacuum; a core of relative permeability μᵣ multiplies it by μᵣ.
solution.why_others_wrong: 25 μH leaves out the core (μᵣ = 1). 13 μH uses N instead of N². 0.50 mH forgets to divide by the length.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', inductance (self-inductance of a long solenoid)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: When a series LCR circuit is driven at a frequency above its resonant frequency, the current leads the applied voltage.
Statement II: Above the resonant frequency, the capacitive reactance of a series LCR circuit is greater than its inductive reactance.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: X_L = ωL grows and X_C = 1/(ωC) falls as ω increases
solution.explanation: At resonance X_L = X_C. Above resonance ω is larger, so X_L > X_C (Statement II false). The circuit is then inductive and the current lags behind the voltage (Statement I false).
steps: Above ω₀: X_L > X_C → II false
Inductive circuit → current lags → I false
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements describe the circuit below resonance, where X_C > X_L and the current leads; above resonance both are reversed.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Alternating Current', series LCR circuit (phasor diagram)
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both Statement I and Statement II are false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
The magnetic flux Φ linked with a closed coil varies with time t as given in List-I (a, b, Φ₀ and ω are positive constants). Match each case with the behaviour of the emf induced in the coil (List-II).

List-I:
A. Φ = at
B. Φ = bt²
C. Φ = Φ₀ sin ωt
D. Φ = Φ₀ (constant)

List-II:
I. Zero at all times
II. Constant and non-zero
III. Proportional to the time t
IV. Sinusoidal, with its largest magnitude at the instants when the flux is zero

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Faraday's law ε = −dΦ/dt
solution.explanation: Differentiate each flux. Φ = at gives ε = −a (constant). Φ = bt² gives ε = −2bt (proportional to t). Φ = Φ₀ sin ωt gives ε = −Φ₀ω cos ωt, largest when sin ωt = 0, i.e. when the flux is zero. A constant flux induces no emf.
steps: C: dΦ/dt = Φ₀ω cos ωt → IV
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes confuse the flux with the emf: the emf depends on the rate of change of flux, not on its value, so a uniformly rising flux gives a constant emf and a steady flux gives none.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', Faraday's law of induction
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In an AC circuit the applied voltage and the current are v = 200 sin ωt volt and i = 5.0 sin(ωt − π/3) ampere. The instantaneous power supplied to the circuit at the instant when ωt = π/2, and the average power over a complete cycle, are respectively:

solution.concept: Instantaneous power p = vi; average power P = V_rms I_rms cos φ = ½V₀I₀ cos φ
solution.explanation: At ωt = π/2 the voltage is at its peak, 200 V, and the current is 5.0 sin(π/2 − π/3) = 5.0 sin(π/6) = 2.5 A. The average power uses the phase difference φ = π/3.
solution.why_others_wrong: '500 W and 500 W' forgets the power factor in the average. 1000 W multiplies the two peak values, but the current is not at its peak at that instant. 866 W uses cos(π/6) instead of sin(π/6) for the current.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Alternating Current', power in AC circuit: the power factor

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A metal rod lies across two smooth, horizontal, parallel conducting rails 0.50 m apart, which are joined at one end through a 2.0 Ω resistor; the rod and rails have negligible resistance. A uniform vertical magnetic field of 0.50 T acts on the region. A constant horizontal force of 0.50 N, along the rails, is applied to the rod, which starts from rest. The speed that the rod finally attains is:

solution.concept: Motional emf Blv, current Blv/R, opposing force B²l²v/R; terminal speed when the forces balance
solution.explanation: As the rod speeds up, the induced current I = Blv/R grows and so does the opposing magnetic force BIl = B²l²v/R (Lenz's law). The rod stops accelerating when this force equals the applied force.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4.0 m/s uses Bl instead of B²l². 8.0 m/s and 32 m/s bring in a spurious factor of 1/2 or 2 in the balance of forces; at the terminal speed the applied force simply equals B²l²v/R.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', motional electromotive force; energy consideration

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A 40 Ω resistor, an inductor of reactance 60 Ω and a capacitor of reactance 30 Ω are connected in series to a 250 V (rms) AC supply. The rms voltage across the resistor and inductor taken together (between the free end of the resistor and the far end of the inductor, the two being adjacent) is about:

solution.concept: Impedance Z = √(R² + (X_L − X_C)²); voltage across R and L together = I√(R² + X_L²)
solution.explanation: First find the current from the total impedance. The voltages across R and L are 90° out of phase, so across the pair the voltage is I√(R² + X_L²). It can exceed the supply voltage because the capacitor's voltage is in opposition to the inductor's.
solution.why_others_wrong: 500 V adds V_R and V_L as numbers, ignoring the 90° phase difference. 300 V is the inductor's voltage alone. 250 V assumes no part of a series circuit can have a voltage larger than the supply.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Alternating Current', series LCR circuit (phasor diagram)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
The north pole of a bar magnet is pushed towards a closed coil of wire along the coil's axis. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) The current induced in the coil makes the coil repel the approaching magnet.
(b) The work done by the agent against this repulsion appears as electrical energy in the coil, which is dissipated as heat in its resistance.
(c) If the coil is cut so that the circuit is open, an emf is still induced but no current flows, and the magnet no longer experiences an opposing force.
(d) Pushing the magnet in faster, through the same distance, increases the total charge that flows round the coil.
(e) Pushing the magnet in faster, through the same distance, increases the induced emf.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Lenz's law and conservation of energy; induced charge q = NΔΦ/R
solution.explanation: By Lenz's law the near face of the coil becomes a north pole and repels the magnet (a true). The work done against this force is converted into electrical energy and then into heat (b true). An open coil still has the emf dΦ/dt but no current, so there is no magnetic force on the magnet from it (c true). The emf depends on the rate of change of flux, so it is larger for a faster push (e true), but the total charge q = NΔΦ/R depends only on the total change of flux, which is the same (d false).
steps: (d) q = NΔΦ/R, independent of speed → false
(e) ε = N dΦ/dt larger for faster motion → true
solution.why_others_wrong: Options containing (d) confuse the emf, which grows with speed, with the total charge, which does not. Options leaving out (b) or (e) miss correct statements.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', Lenz's law and conservation of energy

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): A bar magnet is released from rest above a fixed horizontal coil and falls along the coil's axis, right through it. The coil is connected to a voltmeter of very high resistance. The peak emf induced as the magnet leaves the coil is larger in magnitude than the peak emf induced as it enters.
Reason (R): The magnet is moving faster as it leaves the coil, so the magnetic flux through the coil changes more rapidly then.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Faraday's law: emf = rate of change of flux linkage
solution.explanation: The voltmeter draws almost no current, so there is practically no magnetic braking and the magnet keeps accelerating under gravity. As it leaves the coil it is faster than when it entered, the flux falls more quickly than it rose, and the peak emf is larger (and of opposite sign). The greater rate of change of flux is the direct cause.
steps: A: true (larger, opposite-sign peak on leaving)
R: true, and ε ∝ dΦ/dt makes it the reason
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true and the faster change of flux is exactly why the exit peak is larger, so the other options are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', Faraday's law of induction; Lenz's law
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Electromagnetic waves can travel through vacuum.
Reason (R): Like sound waves, electromagnetic waves are vibrations of the particles of a material medium.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Nature of electromagnetic waves
solution.explanation: In an electromagnetic wave the oscillating quantities are the electric and magnetic fields themselves, which sustain each other; no material medium is involved, so the waves travel through vacuum (A true). Sound, by contrast, needs a material medium; R wrongly describes electromagnetic waves as vibrations of particles (R false).
steps: A: true (light reaches us from the Sun through space)
R: false (oscillating E and B fields, no medium)
solution.why_others_wrong: Since R is false, it can neither be true nor explain A.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Waves', electromagnetic waves (nature of electromagnetic waves)
solution.final_answer: Option C: A is true but R is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A pulse of light carrying 6.0 J of energy falls normally on a perfectly reflecting mirror and is reflected back along its path. Taking c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s, the momentum delivered to the mirror is:

solution.concept: Electromagnetic waves carry momentum; light of energy U has momentum U/c
solution.explanation: The incident pulse carries momentum U/c towards the mirror. After reflection it carries U/c away from the mirror, so the change in the light's momentum, and hence the momentum given to the mirror, is 2U/c.
steps: Momentum of the pulse = U/c = 6.0/(3.0 × 10⁸) = 2.0 × 10⁻⁸ kg m/s
Reflection reverses it: Δp = 2U/c = 4.0 × 10⁻⁸ kg m/s
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.0 × 10⁻⁸ kg m/s is the value for a perfectly absorbing surface. 1.8 × 10⁹ multiplies by c instead of dividing. 'Zero' forgets that reversing the light's momentum needs a push from the mirror.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Waves', electromagnetic waves (momentum and radiation pressure)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An oscillating LC circuit with L = 1.0 μH and C = 1.0 pF radiates electromagnetic waves at its natural frequency. Taking c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s, the wavelength of the radiation and the part of the spectrum to which it belongs are:

solution.concept: An oscillating charge radiates at its own frequency; f = 1/(2π√(LC)); λ = c/f
solution.explanation: NCERT explains that an oscillating charge (as in an LC circuit used by Hertz) produces electromagnetic waves of the same frequency. Here f = 1/(2π√(LC)) and λ = c/f. Wavelengths longer than 0.1 m are radio waves.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.30 m leaves out the 2π (and 0.30 m would still be a radio wavelength). 1.9 mm is a slip of 10³ in the wavelength. 12 m multiplies the correct wavelength by 2π.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Waves', electromagnetic waves (sources); electromagnetic spectrum
solution.final_answer: Option A: about 1.9 m; radio waves

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match each quantity in List-I with its expression in List-II. (μ₀, ε₀ = permeability and permittivity of free space; μ, ε = those of a material medium; U = energy of light falling normally on a surface; Φ_E = electric flux.)

List-I:
A. Speed of electromagnetic waves in vacuum
B. Speed of electromagnetic waves in a material medium
C. Momentum delivered to a perfectly reflecting surface by light of energy U
D. Displacement current through a surface

List-II:
I. ε₀ dΦ_E/dt
II. 2U/c
III. 1/√(μ₀ε₀)
IV. 1/√(με)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Maxwell's results for electromagnetic waves; momentum of light; displacement current
solution.explanation: Maxwell's equations give the speed of electromagnetic waves as 1/√(μ₀ε₀) in vacuum (= c) and 1/√(με) in a medium. Light of energy U carries momentum U/c; on perfect reflection its momentum is reversed, so the surface receives 2U/c. Maxwell's displacement current is i_d = ε₀ dΦ_E/dt.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes exchange the vacuum and medium speeds, or the momentum and displacement-current expressions, or give the reflecting surface the absorbed-light value instead of 2U/c.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Waves', displacement current; electromagnetic waves (speed, momentum)
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: When an electromagnetic wave passes from vacuum into a non-magnetic medium of relative permittivity 4, its wavelength in the medium is half its wavelength in vacuum.
Statement II: In that medium, the frequency of the wave is half its frequency in vacuum.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Speed in a medium v = 1/√(με) = c/√(μᵣεᵣ); frequency is fixed by the source
solution.explanation: With μᵣ = 1 and εᵣ = 4, v = c/2. The frequency does not change on entering the medium, so λ = v/f becomes half of its vacuum value (Statement I true, Statement II false).
steps: f unchanged → λ halves → I true
solution.why_others_wrong: It is the wavelength (and the speed) that changes in a medium; the frequency is set by the source.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Waves', electromagnetic waves (speed in a material medium)
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A plane electromagnetic wave travels through vacuum in the −x direction. At a certain point and instant its magnetic field is along the +z direction. The electric field at that point and instant is along:

solution.concept: In a plane electromagnetic wave E, B and the direction of propagation form a right-handed set: E × B is along the direction of travel
solution.explanation: E must be perpendicular to both B (z) and the direction of travel (x), so it is along ±y. E × B must point along −x: (−ŷ) × ẑ = −x̂, while (+ŷ) × ẑ = +x̂.
steps: E ⟂ x and E ⟂ z → E along ±y
solution.why_others_wrong: +y gives E × B along +x, the wrong direction of travel. E cannot be along x (the direction of propagation) or along z (parallel or antiparallel to B), because the wave is transverse with E ⟂ B.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Waves', electromagnetic waves (transverse nature)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A ray of light travelling in water (refractive index 4/3) falls on the plane surface of a glass block (refractive index 1.5) immersed in the water, at an angle of incidence of 30°. The angle of refraction in the glass is about:

solution.concept: Snell's law n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r
solution.explanation: Use the refractive indices of the two media actually involved, water and glass.
solution.why_others_wrong: 34.2° puts the indices the wrong way round (the ray would then bend away from the normal entering a denser medium). 19.5° uses the refractive index of glass with respect to air, as if the ray came from air. 22.0° ignores the glass and treats it as refraction from air into water.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', refraction (Snell's law)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In a compound microscope, the objective forms a real image 10 times as large as the object. The eyepiece has a focal length of 5.0 cm and the final image is formed at infinity. Taking the least distance of distinct vision as 25 cm, the magnifying power of the microscope is:

solution.concept: Magnifying power of a compound microscope m = m_o × m_e; eyepiece (image at infinity) m_e = D/f_e
solution.explanation: The eyepiece acts as a simple microscope viewing the objective's image; with the final image at infinity its angular magnification is D/f_e. The total magnifying power is the product of the two magnifications.
solution.why_others_wrong: 15 adds the magnifications instead of multiplying. 60 uses 1 + D/f_e, which applies when the final image is at the near point, not at infinity. 2 divides the objective's magnification by the focal length.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', optical instruments (compound microscope)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An object stands 20 cm in front of a plane mirror. Keeping the object fixed, the mirror is moved 5.0 cm farther away from it, parallel to itself. The distance between the object and its image is now:

solution.concept: A plane mirror forms the image as far behind it as the object is in front
solution.explanation: After the move the object is 25 cm from the mirror, so the image is 25 cm behind it.
solution.why_others_wrong: 45 cm moves the image by only 5 cm; when the mirror moves 5 cm, the image moves 10 cm. 30 cm adds 10 cm to the object-mirror distance instead of to the object-image distance. 40 cm is the original separation.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', reflection of light by spherical mirrors (plane mirror as f → ∞)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A ray of light passing from air into water bends towards the normal, and measurements show that light travels more slowly in water than in air. Taken together, these two observations:

options.text: supported the corpuscular picture of light, which predicts a smaller speed of light in an optically denser medium
showed that light travels with the same speed in all media
showed that light waves are transverse
supported the wave picture of light, which predicts a smaller speed of light in the medium towards whose normal the ray bends on refraction

solution.concept: Wave and corpuscular explanations of refraction
solution.explanation: When light passes from air into water it bends towards the normal. Huygens' wave theory explains this only if the speed of light in water is less than in air (sin i/sin r = v₁/v₂). The corpuscular model explained the same bending by assuming a greater speed in the denser medium. The measured smaller speed in water therefore agrees with the wave picture and contradicts the corpuscular one.
steps: Bending towards the normal: wave theory needs v₂ < v₁; corpuscular theory needs v₂ > v₁
Measured v_water < v_air → wave theory supported
solution.why_others_wrong: The corpuscular model predicted a larger, not smaller, speed in the denser medium. The speed of light differs from medium to medium. Transverse nature is shown by polarisation, not by speed measurements.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', introduction; refraction of a plane wave
solution.final_answer: Option D: supported the wave picture of light, which predicts a smaller speed of light in the medium towards whose normal the ray bends on refraction

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: For two media 1 and 2, the refractive index of medium 1 with respect to medium 2 and that of medium 2 with respect to medium 1 satisfy n₁₂ × n₂₁ = 1.
Statement II: For three media 1, 2 and 3, n₃₂ = n₃₁ × n₂₁.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Relative refractive index n₂₁ = n₂/n₁ = v₁/v₂
solution.explanation: n₁₂ = n₁/n₂ and n₂₁ = n₂/n₁, so their product is 1 (Statement I true). NCERT gives n₃₂ = n₃₁ × n₁₂: indeed n₃₁ × n₁₂ = (n₃/n₁)(n₁/n₂) = n₃/n₂. The product n₃₁ × n₂₁ = n₃n₂/n₁² is not n₃₂ (Statement II false).
steps: II: n₃₂ = n₃₁ × n₁₂, not n₃₁ × n₂₁ → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II uses n₂₁ where n₁₂ is needed; the two are reciprocals, so II is false and I is true.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', refraction
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Total internal reflection cannot take place when light travels from water into glass.
Reason (R): Glass is optically denser than water (it has a larger refractive index).

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Conditions for total internal reflection
solution.explanation: Total internal reflection is possible only when light goes from an optically denser medium towards an optically rarer one (and the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle). Going from water into glass, the light enters a denser medium and bends towards the normal, so there is no critical angle and total internal reflection cannot occur. R states exactly why.
steps: Denser → rarer is required; here it is rarer → denser → R explains A
solution.why_others_wrong: Both are true and the greater optical density of glass is precisely the reason, so the other options are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', total internal reflection
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The objective of an astronomical telescope has a power of 0.50 D and its eyepiece has a power of 20 D. In normal adjustment (final image at infinity), the magnifying power of the telescope is:

solution.concept: Telescope in normal adjustment m = f_o/f_e; f = 1/P (f in metres)
