solution.explanation: Convert powers to focal lengths: f_o = 1/0.50 = 2.0 m and f_e = 1/20 = 0.05 m. The magnifying power in normal adjustment is f_o/f_e, which equals P_e/P_o.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1/40 inverts the ratio (P_o/P_e). 10 multiplies the two powers. 205 is the length of the telescope in centimetres (f_o + f_e), not its magnifying power.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', optical instruments (telescope); power of a lens

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A concave mirror forms, on a screen, a real image of a small lamp four times as large as the lamp. The screen is 3.0 m from the lamp, and both lie on the principal axis in front of the mirror. The focal length of the mirror is:

solution.concept: Mirror equation 1/v + 1/u = 1/f with |v| = 4|u| and the screen beyond the lamp
solution.explanation: A real image four times the size lies four times as far from the mirror as the lamp. Both are in front of the mirror, so the lamp-screen separation is |v| − |u| = 3|u| = 3.0 m.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.6 m is the radius of curvature. 0.48 m takes |u| + |v| = 3.0 m, as if the lamp and screen were on opposite sides of the mirror. 1.33 m subtracts 1/v from 1/u, a sign slip in the mirror equation.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', reflection of light by spherical mirrors (mirror equation, magnification)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A thin convex lens forms a real image of an object placed 5.0 cm beyond its first principal focus. The image is formed 80 cm beyond the second principal focus, on the other side of the lens. The focal length of the lens is:

solution.concept: Thin lens formula 1/v − 1/u = 1/f with distances measured from the lens
solution.explanation: Let the focal length be f. The object is at u = −(f + 5) cm and the image at v = +(f + 80) cm. Substitute in the lens formula and solve for f.
steps: f² = 400 → f = 20 cm (check: u = −25 cm gives v = +100 cm = f + 80 ✓)
solution.shortcut: Distances measured from the foci satisfy x₁x₂ = f²: f = √(5 × 80) = 20 cm.
solution.why_others_wrong: 42.5 cm averages the two given distances. 4.7 cm puts 5 cm and 80 cm into the lens formula as if they were measured from the lens. 10 cm is half the correct value.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', refraction by a lens (thin lens formula)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A right-angled isosceles glass prism (angles 90°, 45°, 45°; refractive index 1.5) turns a beam through 90° in air by total internal reflection at its hypotenuse face, the beam entering normally through one of the shorter faces. The prism is now placed in water (refractive index 4/3) and used in the same way. At the hypotenuse face, the beam:

options.text: is mainly refracted out into the water, because the critical angle for glass-water (about 63°) is more than 45°
is still totally reflected, because 45° exceeds the critical angle of glass (about 42°)
is still totally reflected, because total internal reflection does not depend on the surrounding medium
passes into the water without any change of direction

solution.concept: Critical angle depends on both media: sin C = n_rarer/n_denser
solution.explanation: The beam meets the hypotenuse at 45°. For glass to air, sin C = 1/1.5 and C ≈ 42°, so 45° > C and the beam is totally reflected. For glass to water, sin C = (4/3)/1.5 = 0.889 and C ≈ 63°. Now 45° < C, so there is no total internal reflection; most of the light is refracted into the water (a little is reflected).
steps: Glass-water: sin C = 0.889, C ≈ 62.7° > 45° → no TIR
solution.why_others_wrong: The 42° critical angle applies only to glass-air. The critical angle depends on the second medium too. At 45° incidence the ray is not along the normal, so it is deviated on refraction.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', total internal reflection (prisms)
solution.final_answer: Option A: is mainly refracted out into the water, because the critical angle for glass-water (about 63°) is more than 45°

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An astronomical telescope has an objective of focal length 100 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 5.0 cm. It is used to view a tower 100 m tall standing 10 km away. The height of the image of the tower formed by the objective is:

solution.concept: A distant object subtending angle α forms an image of height f_o × α in the focal plane of the objective
solution.explanation: The tower subtends a small angle α = 100 m/10 000 m = 0.010 rad at the objective. Its image is formed at the focal plane of the objective with height f_o α. The eyepiece plays no part in forming this image.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.050 cm uses the eyepiece focal length. 20 cm multiplies by the magnifying power f_o/f_e, but that applies to the angle subtended by the final image, not to the size of the objective's image. 0.10 cm slips a factor of 10 in converting 10 km.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', optical instruments (telescope)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: A thin convex lens of glass (refractive index 1.5) has a smaller power when it is immersed in water (refractive index 4/3) than when it is in air.
Statement II: A small spherical air bubble inside water behaves as a diverging lens.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Lens maker's formula with relative refractive index: 1/f = (n_rel − 1)(1/R₁ − 1/R₂)
solution.explanation: In air n_rel − 1 = 0.5; in water n_rel − 1 = 1.5/(4/3) − 1 = 0.125, so the power falls to a quarter (Statement I true). An air bubble is a 'biconvex lens' of a medium (air) rarer than its surroundings, so n_rel < 1 and its focal length is negative: it diverges light (Statement II true).
steps: II: convex shape with n_rel = 3/4 < 1 → diverging → true
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements follow from the lens maker's formula with the refractive index taken relative to the surrounding medium.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', refraction by a lens (lens maker's formula)
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): A convex mirror can form a real image of a real object if the object is placed close enough to the mirror.
Reason (R): In the Cartesian sign convention, the focal length of a convex mirror is positive.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Images formed by a convex mirror
solution.explanation: For a real object (u negative) and a convex mirror (f positive), 1/v = 1/f − 1/u is always positive, so v is positive: the image is always virtual, erect, diminished and behind the mirror, wherever the object is. A is false. R is true: the focus of a convex mirror lies behind it, on the side opposite to the incident light.
steps: R: f measured behind the mirror → positive → true
solution.why_others_wrong: A is false for every object position, so the options that take A as true are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', reflection of light by spherical mirrors (sign convention; mirror equation)
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Unpolarised light of intensity I₀ falls on the arrangement of ideal polaroids described in List-I. Match each arrangement with the intensity of the light that finally emerges (List-II).

List-I:
A. A single polaroid
B. Two polaroids with their pass axes at 60° to each other
C. Two polaroids with their pass axes at 45° to each other
D. Two polaroids with their pass axes at 30° to each other

List-II:
I. I₀/4
II. 3I₀/8
III. I₀/2
IV. I₀/8

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: First polaroid halves unpolarised light; Malus's law I = I₁ cos² θ for the second
solution.explanation: Any single ideal polaroid transmits half the intensity of unpolarised light, whatever its orientation. The light leaving it is plane polarised, and a second polaroid at angle θ transmits the fraction cos² θ of it.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes exchange the 60° and 30° cases (cos² 60° = 1/4 while cos² 30° = 3/4), or treat a single polaroid as passing a quarter of the light.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', polarisation (Malus's law)
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A small object is placed on the principal axis of a concave mirror of focal length 12 cm. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) With the object 18 cm from the mirror, the image is formed 36 cm in front of the mirror.
(b) With the object 18 cm from the mirror, the magnification is −2.
(c) With the object 8.0 cm from the mirror, the image is formed 24 cm behind the mirror.
(d) With the object 8.0 cm from the mirror, the image is smaller than the object.
(e) With the object 18 cm from the mirror, the image is virtual.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Mirror equation 1/v + 1/u = 1/f (Cartesian convention, f = −12 cm), m = −v/u
solution.explanation: Object at 18 cm (u = −18): 1/v = −1/12 + 1/18 = −1/36, so v = −36 cm, a real image in front of the mirror (a true, e false), with m = −v/u = −2 (b true). Object at 8.0 cm, between F and the pole (u = −8): 1/v = −1/12 + 1/8 = 1/24, so v = +24 cm behind the mirror (c true) and m = −24/(−8) = +3, an enlarged virtual image (d false).
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (d) forget that an object between F and P gives an enlarged virtual image; options with (e) call the real image at 36 cm virtual.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', reflection of light by spherical mirrors

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A thin equiconvex lens made of glass of refractive index 1.5 has a focal length of 30 cm in air. A lens of exactly the same shape is made from glass of refractive index 1.6. Its focal length in air is:

solution.concept: Lens maker's formula 1/f = (n − 1)(1/R₁ − 1/R₂): for the same surfaces f ∝ 1/(n − 1)
solution.explanation: The radii of curvature are the same, so only the factor (n − 1) changes, from 0.5 to 0.6.
solution.why_others_wrong: 36 cm inverts the ratio of (n − 1) values. 28.1 cm and 32 cm scale the focal length by n instead of by (n − 1).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', refraction by a lens (lens maker's formula)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In a Young's double-slit experiment with light of wavelength 600 nm, a point P on the screen is at the centre of the fifth bright fringe from the central bright fringe. Keeping everything else unchanged, the light is replaced by light of another wavelength. For which of the following wavelengths will P lie at the centre of a dark fringe?

solution.concept: Path difference fixed by the geometry: bright when Δ = nλ, dark when Δ = (n + ½)λ
solution.explanation: The path difference at P depends only on the positions of the slits and of P: Δ = 5 × 600 nm = 3000 nm. P is dark for a new wavelength λ if 3000 nm = (n + ½)λ for some whole number n.
steps: Dark: λ = 3000/(n + ½); n = 5 gives λ ≈ 545 nm
500 nm (Δ = 6λ), 600 nm (Δ = 5λ) and 3000/7 ≈ 429 nm (Δ = 7λ) all give bright fringes at P
solution.why_others_wrong: 500 nm and about 429 nm make the path difference a whole number of wavelengths (6λ and 7λ), so P stays bright, as it does for 600 nm itself (5λ).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', interference of light waves and Young's experiment

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Light of wavelength 600 nm falls normally on a single slit of width 2.5 μm. A screen surrounds the slit far away, so that light leaving the slit at any angle up to 90° on either side of the central direction can be observed. The total number of dark fringes (minima of intensity) in the diffraction pattern is:

solution.concept: Single-slit minima: a sin θ = nλ (n = ±1, ±2, ...), with |sin θ| ≤ 1
solution.explanation: Minima occur where a sin θ = nλ. Since sin θ cannot exceed 1, the order n can be at most a/λ = 2.5 μm/0.60 μm ≈ 4.2, so n = 1, 2, 3 and 4 on each side.
steps: 4 minima on each side → 8 in all
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 counts only one side of the central maximum. 16 uses a sin θ = nλ/2, the condition for interference between two halves, not for the minima of the whole slit. 9 counts the central maximum as a dark fringe.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', diffraction (the single slit)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An equilateral prism (refracting angle 60°) is made of glass of refractive index 1.5. It is completely immersed in water (refractive index 4/3). Using sin 34.2° ≈ 0.5625 and sin 48.6° ≈ 0.75, the angle of minimum deviation of the prism in water is about:

solution.concept: Prism formula with relative refractive index: n_rel = sin[(A + δ_m)/2]/sin(A/2)
solution.explanation: In water the bending at each face depends on the refractive index of glass relative to water, n_rel = 1.5/(4/3) = 1.125.
solution.why_others_wrong: 37.2° is the minimum deviation in air (using sin 48.6° = 0.75 with n = 1.5). 68.5° forgets to subtract the prism angle. 34.2° takes (A + δ_m)/2 itself as the deviation.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', refraction through a prism

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Unpolarised light of intensity I₀ passes through a fixed ideal polaroid P₁ and then through a second ideal polaroid P₂, which is rotated steadily in its own plane. The intensity of the light emerging from P₂, averaged over one complete rotation of P₂, is:

solution.concept: Malus's law I = I₁ cos² θ; the average of cos² θ over a full turn is 1/2
solution.explanation: P₁ passes I₀/2, plane polarised. As P₂ turns, the transmitted intensity is (I₀/2) cos² θ, varying between I₀/2 and zero. The average of cos² θ over a full rotation is 1/2.
solution.why_others_wrong: I₀/2 is the maximum (θ = 0), not the average. I₀/8 is the value at θ = 60°. Zero is the minimum (θ = 90°).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', polarisation (Malus's law)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A thin equiconvex glass lens (refractive index 1.5), each face of radius of curvature 20 cm, forms the bottom of a tank: air is below the lens and water (refractive index 4/3) fills the tank above it. A parallel beam of light travels vertically upwards from below, along the axis of the lens. The beam is brought to a focus in the water at a distance from the lens of:

solution.concept: Refraction at a spherical surface: n₂/v − n₁/u = (n₂ − n₁)/R, applied at each face
solution.explanation: The two faces separate different media (air-glass and glass-water), so the ordinary thin-lens formula in air cannot be used. Apply the single-surface formula twice, taking the direction of the light as positive.
steps: Face 1 (air → glass, R = +20 cm, u = ∞): 1.5/v₁ = 0.5/20 → v₁ = 60 cm
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 cm is the focal length with air on both sides. 80 cm is the focal length with water on both sides. 26.7 cm simply multiplies the focal length in air by 4/3, which does not follow from the surface formula.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', refraction at spherical surfaces and by lenses

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
In a Young's double-slit experiment with monochromatic light, each slit alone would produce an intensity I₀ at the central point O of the screen (equidistant from the slits). Match each arrangement in List-I with the intensity at O (List-II).

List-I:
A. Both slits open, as described
B. A filter placed over one slit reduces the intensity of the light from it to one-quarter, with no change of phase
C. A thin transparent sheet over one slit (no absorption) adds an extra optical path of half a wavelength
D. One slit is closed

List-II:
I. Zero
II. I₀
III. 9I₀/4
IV. 4I₀

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Superposition of amplitudes: I ∝ (a₁ + a₂)² for waves in phase, (a₁ − a₂)² for waves in antiphase
solution.explanation: Intensities add as squared amplitudes. With equal amplitudes a in phase at O: (2a)² → 4I₀. A quarter of the intensity means half the amplitude: (a + a/2)² → 9I₀/4. An extra half wavelength puts the waves in antiphase at O: (a − a)² = 0. With one slit closed there is no interference: I₀.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes add the filtered intensities directly (I₀ + I₀/4) instead of the amplitudes, or forget that a half-wavelength shift turns the central bright point dark.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', coherent and incoherent addition of waves; interference
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-IV, B-III, C-I, D-II

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Two thin convex lenses L₁ (focal length 20 cm) and L₂ (focal length 10 cm) are placed coaxially 10 cm apart. A parallel beam of light travelling along the common axis falls on L₁. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) The beam is brought to a focus 5.0 cm beyond L₂.
(b) If the two lenses were placed in contact, the focal length of the combination would be about 6.7 cm.
(c) The beam comes to a focus closer to L₂ than the point where L₁ alone would focus it.
(d) If the separation of the lenses were made 30 cm, the beam would emerge from L₂ as a parallel beam.
(e) The power of the two lenses in contact is 5 D.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Two-lens system: the image by L₁ is the object for L₂; lenses in contact: P = P₁ + P₂
solution.explanation: L₁ alone focuses the beam 20 cm beyond it, i.e. 10 cm beyond L₂. For L₂ this is a virtual object at u = +10 cm: 1/v = 1/10 + 1/10, so v = 5.0 cm (a true), which is closer than 10 cm (c true). In contact, 1/f = 1/20 + 1/10 = 3/20, f ≈ 6.7 cm (b true), and P = 1/0.0667 m = 15 D, not 5 D (e false). With a separation of 30 cm the focus of L₁ coincides with the first focus of L₂, so the light leaves L₂ parallel (d true).
solution.why_others_wrong: Options containing (e) subtract instead of adding the powers (or use one lens only). Options leaving out (a) or (d) miss correct results of the two-lens calculation.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', refraction by a lens (combination of thin lenses)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text: An electron (mass 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg) moves with a speed of 1.0 × 10⁶ m/s. Taking h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, its de Broglie wavelength is about:

solution.concept: de Broglie relation λ = h/p = h/(mv)
solution.explanation: For a non-relativistic particle the momentum is mv, and the associated wavelength is h divided by it.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.36 nm divides by 2mv. 7.3 nm is out by a factor of 10 in converting metres to nanometres. 4.1 × 10⁻⁴ nm uses the proton mass instead of the electron mass.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', wave nature of matter

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text: The work function of a metal surface is 4.5 eV. Ultraviolet light of wavelength 300 nm falls on it. Taking hc = 1240 eV nm, which statement is correct?

options.text: Photoelectrons are emitted with kinetic energies up to about 0.4 eV
Photoelectrons are emitted if the light is made intense enough
No photoelectrons are emitted, because each photon carries only about 4.1 eV
Photoelectrons are emitted with kinetic energies up to about 4.1 eV

solution.concept: Einstein's photoelectric equation: emission needs hν ≥ φ₀
solution.explanation: Each photon gives its energy to a single electron. A photon of 300 nm carries hc/λ = 1240/300 ≈ 4.13 eV, which is less than the 4.5 eV needed to free an electron, so no electron can escape, however many photons arrive.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Up to about 0.4 eV' subtracts the energies the wrong way round. Intensity only changes the number of photons, not the energy of each, so brighter light cannot cause emission. 'Up to 4.1 eV' ignores the work function altogether.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', Einstein's photoelectric equation: energy quantum of radiation
solution.final_answer: Option C: No photoelectrons are emitted, because each photon carries only about 4.1 eV

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: If the frequency of the light falling on a photosensitive surface is doubled, the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted photoelectrons is also doubled.
Statement II: The stopping potential varies linearly with the frequency of the incident light (above the threshold frequency).

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: K_max = hν − φ₀ and eV₀ = hν − φ₀
solution.explanation: K_max is a linear function of ν with a negative intercept −φ₀, not proportional to ν. Doubling ν gives 2hν − φ₀, which is more than twice hν − φ₀ (Statement I false). V₀ = (h/e)ν − φ₀/e is a straight line of slope h/e (Statement II true).
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement I would hold only if the work function were zero; linear is not the same as proportional.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', Einstein's photoelectric equation
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text: A small lamp, acting as a point source of monochromatic light, is placed 1.0 m from the emitter of a photocell and gives a measurable photocurrent. The lamp is then moved to a distance of 0.50 m, all else being unchanged. As a result:

options.text: the saturation photocurrent becomes about four times as large, and the stopping potential is unchanged
the saturation photocurrent doubles, and the stopping potential is unchanged
both the saturation photocurrent and the stopping potential become about four times as large
the saturation photocurrent is unchanged, and the stopping potential doubles

solution.concept: Photocurrent ∝ intensity; stopping potential depends only on frequency (and the metal)
solution.explanation: For a point source the intensity at the emitter varies as 1/r², so halving the distance makes it four times as large. Four times as many photons per second eject about four times as many electrons, so the saturation current becomes about four times. The energy of each photon (the frequency) is unchanged, so the maximum kinetic energy and the stopping potential do not change.
steps: V₀ depends on ν only → unchanged
solution.why_others_wrong: Doubling would follow from 1/r, not 1/r². The stopping potential does not depend on intensity, so options that change it are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', experimental study of photoelectric effect (effect of intensity)
solution.final_answer: Option A: the saturation photocurrent becomes about four times as large, and the stopping potential is unchanged

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text: A proton and an alpha particle move with equal kinetic energies (both much slower than light). Taking the mass of the alpha particle as 4 times that of the proton, the ratio of the de Broglie wavelength of the proton to that of the alpha particle is:

solution.concept: λ = h/p = h/√(2mK)
solution.explanation: With equal kinetic energies, λ ∝ 1/√m. The lighter proton has the smaller momentum and so the longer wavelength.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 : 2 inverts the ratio. 4 : 1 uses λ ∝ 1/m, which holds for equal speeds, not equal energies. 2√2 : 1 is the ratio for particles accelerated through the same potential difference (which gives the alpha particle twice the energy).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', wave nature of matter

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text: When light of wavelength 400 nm falls on a metal surface, the fastest photoelectrons have a kinetic energy of 1.0 eV. Taking hc = 1240 eV nm, the threshold wavelength for this metal is about:

solution.concept: K_max = hc/λ − φ₀; threshold wavelength λ₀ = hc/φ₀
solution.explanation: Find the photon energy, subtract the maximum kinetic energy to get the work function, then convert the work function to the threshold wavelength.
solution.why_others_wrong: 400 nm is the wavelength used, which gives emission with energy to spare, so the threshold is longer. 1240 nm treats the 1.0 eV kinetic energy as the work function. 300 nm adds the kinetic energy to the photon energy instead of subtracting it.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', Einstein's photoelectric equation

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): A photon and an electron that have the same energy also have the same wavelength.
Reason (R): For a photon as well as for an electron, the wavelength and the momentum are related by λ = h/p.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Photon: p = E/c; electron: p = √(2mK)
solution.explanation: R is true: λ = h/p holds for both. But equal energies do not mean equal momenta. A photon of energy E has p = E/c, while an electron of kinetic energy E has p = √(2mE). For E of a few eV the electron's momentum is far larger, so its wavelength is far shorter (for example about 0.9 nm against about 620 nm at 2 eV). A is false.
steps: R: λ = h/p for both → true
A: p_photon = E/c ≠ p_electron = √(2mE) → different λ → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Equal energies give equal wavelengths only if the momenta are equal, which they are not; so A is false and R is true.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', wave nature of matter; particle nature of light: the photon
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text: A photon has the same momentum (and hence the same wavelength) as an electron of kinetic energy 2.5 eV. Taking the rest-mass energy of the electron, mc², as 0.511 MeV and √2.56 = 1.6, the energy of the photon is about:

solution.concept: Electron: p = √(2mK); photon: E = pc
solution.explanation: Equal momenta: E_photon = pc = c√(2mK) = √(2mc² K). Working in electron volts avoids converting units.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.5 eV assumes equal energies give equal momenta. 1.1 keV leaves out the factor 2 in p = √(2mK). 5.0 eV doubles the electron's energy, which has no basis.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', wave nature of matter; the photon

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text:
Photons of energy 3.0 eV fall on the emitter of a photocell, whose work function is 2.0 eV. Take hc = 1240 eV nm. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) The stopping potential is 1.0 V.
(b) The threshold wavelength of the emitter is 620 nm.
(c) If the intensity of the light is doubled (same photon energy), the stopping potential is still 1.0 V.
(d) If the collector is held at +2.0 V relative to the emitter, the fastest electrons reach it with 3.0 eV of kinetic energy.
(e) Light of wavelength 600 nm would not eject any photoelectrons from this emitter.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: eV₀ = hν − φ₀; λ₀ = hc/φ₀; an accelerating potential adds eV to the kinetic energy
solution.explanation: K_max = 3.0 − 2.0 = 1.0 eV, so V₀ = 1.0 V (a true). λ₀ = 1240/2.0 = 620 nm (b true). Intensity does not affect V₀ (c true). An accelerating potential of 2.0 V adds 2.0 eV, so the fastest electrons arrive with 3.0 eV (d true). Light of 600 nm is shorter than the 620 nm threshold; its photons carry 1240/600 ≈ 2.07 eV > 2.0 eV, so it does eject electrons (e false).
solution.why_others_wrong: Options containing (e) forget that any wavelength shorter than the threshold wavelength causes emission. Options leaving out (d) miss that the collector potential adds to the kinetic energy.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', photoelectric effect; Einstein's photoelectric equation

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text: When light of frequency ν falls on a metal, the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons is K. When the frequency is increased by 50% (to 1.5ν), the maximum kinetic energy becomes 2K. The threshold frequency of the metal is:

solution.concept: Einstein's equation K_max = h(ν − ν₀)
solution.explanation: Write the equation for both frequencies and eliminate K.
steps: h(ν − ν₀) = K and h(1.5ν − ν₀) = 2K
solution.why_others_wrong: ν/4, 2ν/3 and ν/3 come from algebraic slips; substituting any of them back does not double K when ν rises by 50% (for example ν₀ = ν/3 gives K = 2hν/3 and 7hν/6, a ratio of 7/4).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', Einstein's photoelectric equation

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Which of the following conclusions could NOT be drawn from the alpha-particle scattering experiment of Geiger and Marsden by itself?

options.text: Electrons revolve round the nucleus only in certain stationary orbits, without radiating energy
Most of the space inside an atom is empty
The positive charge and most of the mass of an atom are concentrated in a tiny central region
The nucleus is very much smaller than the atom as a whole

solution.concept: Rutherford's nuclear model and Bohr's postulates
solution.explanation: The scattering results show that most alpha particles pass straight through (mostly empty space), that a few are deflected through large angles (a tiny, massive, positively charged nucleus) and give an estimate of the nuclear size. They say nothing about how the electrons move; stationary non-radiating orbits are Bohr's postulate, introduced later to explain the stability of atoms and the line spectrum of hydrogen.
steps: Empty space, concentrated positive mass, small nucleus → from scattering
Stationary orbits → Bohr's postulate, not from scattering
solution.why_others_wrong: The other three are exactly the conclusions Rutherford drew from the scattering data.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Atoms', alpha-particle scattering and Rutherford's nuclear model of atom; Bohr model
solution.final_answer: Option A: Electrons revolve round the nucleus only in certain stationary orbits, without radiating energy

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: According to the Bohr model, the ratio of the ionisation energies of the hydrogen atom (H), the singly ionised helium ion (He⁺) and the doubly ionised lithium ion (Li²⁺), each in its ground state, is:

solution.concept: Bohr energy of a hydrogen-like ion E_n = −13.6 Z²/n² eV
solution.explanation: In the ground state (n = 1) the ionisation energy is 13.6 Z² eV, so it is proportional to Z², with Z = 1, 2 and 3.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 : 2 : 3 uses Z instead of Z². 9 : 4 : 1 inverts the ratio. 1 : 8 : 27 uses Z³.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Atoms', Bohr model of the hydrogen atom (hydrogen-like ions)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The energy released in the fission of one ²³⁵U nucleus is of the order of 200 MeV.
Statement II: The binding energy per nucleon of the nuclei produced in the fission of ²³⁵U is greater than that of the uranium nucleus.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Fission releases energy because the fragments are more tightly bound
solution.explanation: NCERT gives the energy released per fission of ²³⁵U as about 200 MeV (Statement I true). It arises because the binding energy per nucleon rises from about 7.6 MeV for uranium to about 8.5 MeV for the medium-mass fragments (Statement II true).
steps: II: ~8.5 MeV vs ~7.6 MeV per nucleon → true
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are standard NCERT results, and the second explains the first.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Nuclei', nuclear energy (fission)
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The wavelength of the photon emitted when a hydrogen atom makes the transition from n = 2 to n = 1 is 121.6 nm. In the Bohr model, the wavelength of the photon emitted in the same transition (n = 2 to n = 1) by a He⁺ ion is:

solution.concept: For hydrogen-like ions, transition energies scale as Z², so wavelengths scale as 1/Z²
solution.explanation: The energy levels of He⁺ (Z = 2) are 4 times those of hydrogen, so the same transition emits a photon of 4 times the energy and one-quarter the wavelength.
solution.why_others_wrong: 60.8 nm divides by Z instead of Z². 486 nm multiplies by 4 instead of dividing. 13.5 nm divides by 9, as for Li²⁺.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Atoms', Bohr model (hydrogen-like ions); line spectra

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A sample of hydrogen atoms is excited so that the atoms are in the n = 5 state. As they return to lower states by all possible transitions, the number of different lines of the Balmer series that can appear in the emission spectrum is:

solution.concept: Balmer lines are transitions ending on n = 2
solution.explanation: Every Balmer line ends on n = 2 and starts from a higher level. From the levels available (n = 3, 4 and 5) there are three such transitions: 5 → 2, 4 → 2 and 3 → 2.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10 is the total number of lines of all series from n = 5 (5 × 4/2). 4 counts the levels from 2 to 5 rather than the transitions ending on n = 2. 6 is the total for atoms starting from n = 4.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Atoms', line spectra of the hydrogen atom

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: He⁺ ions (Z = 2) are excited to the n = 4 state. In the Bohr model their energy levels are E_n = −54.4/n² eV. Taking hc = 1240 eV nm and the visible region as 400 nm to 700 nm, which transition gives a photon of visible light?

solution.concept: Photon energy = difference of levels; λ = hc/ΔE
solution.explanation: Compute the photon energies of the transitions from n = 4 and below. Only a photon of energy between about 1.8 eV and 3.1 eV is visible.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other three transitions are real but their photons (10.2 eV, 7.56 eV, 40.8 eV) lie far in the ultraviolet.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Atoms', Bohr model (hydrogen-like ions); line spectra
solution.final_answer: Option A: n = 4 → n = 3, about 469 nm

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A nucleus of mass number A splits into two fragments of equal mass number. Using R = R₀A^(1/3) for each nucleus, the ratio of the radius of each fragment to the radius of the original nucleus is about:

solution.concept: Nuclear radius R ∝ A^(1/3) (constant nuclear density)
solution.explanation: Each fragment has mass number A/2, so its radius is R₀(A/2)^(1/3) = (1/2)^(1/3) times the original radius.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.50 takes the radius proportional to A. 0.71 uses (1/2)^(1/2). 0.63 uses (1/2)^(2/3), the ratio of the surface areas, not the radii.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Nuclei', size of the nucleus

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match each pair of nuclides in List-I with the relation between them (List-II).

List-I:
A. ⁴⁰₁₈Ar and ⁴⁰₂₀Ca
B. ³⁵₁₇Cl and ³⁷₁₇Cl
C. ¹³₆C and ¹⁴₇N
D. ⁷₃Li and ¹²₆C

List-II:
I. Isotones
II. Isobars
III. None of these relations
IV. Isotopes

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Isotopes: same Z; isobars: same A; isotones: same N = A − Z
solution.explanation: Compare Z, A and N = A − Z for each pair.
steps: D: Z 3 vs 6, N 4 vs 6, A 7 vs 12 → none
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes exchange isobars and isotopes (same A versus same Z) or miss that ¹³C and ¹⁴N have the same number of neutrons.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Nuclei', atomic masses and composition of nucleus
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): In the Bohr model, the radius of the ground-state orbit of the He⁺ ion is half the radius of the ground-state orbit of the hydrogen atom.
Reason (R): In the Bohr model, the orbit radius of a hydrogen-like ion is proportional to n²/Z².

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Bohr radius for a hydrogen-like ion r_n = (0.53 Å) n²/Z
solution.explanation: The Coulomb attraction is Z times stronger, and the quantisation condition gives r_n ∝ n²/Z. For He⁺ (Z = 2) in n = 1 the radius is half that of hydrogen (A true). R states n²/Z², which is the dependence of the energy (on Z²) confused with the radius; it would give a quarter, not a half (R false).
solution.why_others_wrong: Since R is false, it cannot be the explanation of A, and A itself is true.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Atoms', Bohr model of the hydrogen atom
solution.final_answer: Option C: A is true but R is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: For the nuclear reaction ¹⁴₇N + ⁴₂He → ¹⁷₈O + ¹₁H, the atomic masses are ¹⁴N = 14.003074 u, ⁴He = 4.002603 u, ¹⁷O = 16.999132 u and ¹H = 1.007825 u. Taking 1 u = 931.5 MeV/c², the Q-value of the reaction is about:

options.text: zero, because the number of nucleons is conserved

solution.concept: Q = (total initial mass − total final mass) c²
solution.explanation: Electron masses cancel because the atomic numbers balance (7 + 2 = 8 + 1). The products are heavier than the reactants, so Q is negative: kinetic energy must be supplied (by the alpha particle) for the reaction to occur.
solution.why_others_wrong: +1.19 MeV gets the sign wrong: the mass increases, so energy is absorbed. −1.28 MeV converts the mass difference as if 1 u were 1000 MeV. Conservation of nucleon number does not make Q zero; Q comes from the change in mass (binding energy).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Nuclei', mass-energy and nuclear binding energy
solution.final_answer: Option D: −1.19 MeV; the reaction absorbs energy

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A photon of energy 15.0 eV is absorbed by a hydrogen atom in its ground state (E₁ = −13.6 eV), and the electron is ejected. Neglecting the recoil of the proton and using λ = 1.227/√K nm for an electron of kinetic energy K (in eV), the de Broglie wavelength of the ejected electron is about:

solution.concept: Energy conservation: K = hν − (ionisation energy); de Broglie wavelength λ = h/√(2mK)
solution.explanation: 13.6 eV of the photon's energy is used to free the electron from the ground state; the rest appears as the kinetic energy of the electron.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.32 nm uses the whole 15.0 eV as kinetic energy. 0.88 nm divides by K instead of √K. 83 nm is the wavelength of the photon (1240/15), not of the electron.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Atoms', Bohr model (ionisation energy); Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', wave nature of matter

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
In the Bohr model, the energy levels of a hydrogen-like ion are E_n = −13.6 Z²/n² eV. Match each ion and state in List-I with the energy needed to remove its electron from that state (List-II).

List-I:
A. Hydrogen atom, n = 2
B. He⁺ ion, n = 2
C. Li²⁺ ion, n = 2
D. He⁺ ion, n = 3

List-II:
I. 13.6 eV
II. 6.04 eV
III. 3.4 eV
IV. 30.6 eV

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Ionisation energy from level n = 13.6 Z²/n² eV
solution.explanation: The energy needed to remove the electron from level n is |E_n| = 13.6 Z²/n² eV.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes exchange hydrogen's n = 2 value with He⁺'s, or the Li²⁺ and He⁺ (n = 3) values, by using Z instead of Z² or n instead of n².
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Atoms', Bohr model (energy levels of hydrogen-like ions)
solution.final_answer: Option A: A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Consider the reaction ²₁H + ³₁H → ⁴₂He + ¹₀n, which releases 17.6 MeV. Take 1 u = 931.5 MeV/c². Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) It is a fusion reaction.
(b) The total number of nucleons is the same (five) on both sides.
(c) The total mass of the products is less than that of the reactants by about 0.019 u.
(d) The reaction takes place readily at room temperature, because the nuclear force between the nuclei is attractive.
(e) The energy released per nucleon of the reacting nuclei is greater than in the fission of a ²³⁵U nucleus (about 200 MeV per fission).

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Fusion of light nuclei; mass-energy relation; Coulomb barrier
solution.explanation: Two light nuclei combine into a heavier one (a true); nucleon number is conserved, 2 + 3 = 4 + 1 (b true). The mass that disappears is 17.6/931.5 ≈ 0.019 u (c true). The nuclei are both positively charged; they must be brought within the very short range of the nuclear force against their Coulomb repulsion, which needs temperatures of the order of 10⁷ K or more, so the reaction does not occur at room temperature (d false). Per nucleon, fusion gives 17.6/5 ≈ 3.5 MeV, against about 200/236 ≈ 0.85 MeV for fission (e true).
steps: (d) Coulomb barrier needs very high temperature → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (d) ignore the Coulomb repulsion between the nuclei, which the short-range nuclear force cannot overcome at ordinary temperatures. Options leaving out (b) or (e) miss correct statements.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Nuclei', nuclear energy (fusion - energy generation in stars)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An ideal junction diode is connected in series with a 1.0 kΩ resistor across an ideal 5.0 V battery, the diode being reverse biased. The potential difference across the diode is:

solution.concept: An ideal diode has infinite resistance in reverse bias
solution.explanation: A reverse-biased ideal diode lets no current flow. With zero current, there is no potential drop across the resistor (V = IR = 0), so the whole battery voltage appears across the diode.
solution.why_others_wrong: Zero would be the drop across an ideal diode in forward bias. 0.7 V is the forward drop of a real silicon diode. 2.5 V assumes the voltage is shared equally, as between two equal resistors.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', p-n junction diode under reverse bias; ideal diode

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An LED is to emit green light of wavelength about 540 nm. The photon energy of an LED is about equal to the band gap of its semiconductor. Taking hc = 1240 eV nm, which of the following semiconductors, identified by their band gaps, is suitable?

options.text: A semiconductor with a band gap of 1.1 eV
A semiconductor with a band gap of 2.3 eV
A semiconductor with a band gap of 1.4 eV
A semiconductor with a band gap of 3.1 eV

solution.concept: LED: emitted photon energy hc/λ ≈ E_g
solution.explanation: In an LED the light comes from electrons and holes recombining across the band gap, so each photon carries an energy close to E_g. The band gap needed is therefore hc/λ.
steps: 1.1 eV → about 1130 nm, 1.4 eV → about 890 nm (both infrared); 3.1 eV → 400 nm (violet)
solution.why_others_wrong: Band gaps of 1.1 eV and 1.4 eV give infrared photons, invisible to the eye. A band gap of 3.1 eV gives violet light near 400 nm, not green.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', optoelectronic junction devices (light emitting diode)
solution.final_answer: Option B: A semiconductor with a band gap of 2.3 eV

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: A solar cell is a p-n junction that generates an emf when solar radiation falls on it.
Statement II: The three basic processes by which a solar cell generates an emf are the generation of electron-hole pairs by light, the separation of the electrons and holes by the junction field, and their collection at the electrodes.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Working of a solar cell
solution.explanation: NCERT describes the solar cell as a p-n junction that generates emf when solar radiation falls on it, working on the same principle as the photodiode but without any external bias (Statement I true). It lists the three basic processes: generation, separation and collection (Statement II true).
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are taken directly from NCERT's description of the solar cell.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', optoelectronic junction devices (solar cell)
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): At room temperature, the intrinsic carrier concentration of germanium is much larger than that of silicon.
Reason (R): Germanium, like silicon, is an elemental semiconductor.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Intrinsic carrier concentration depends on the band gap
solution.explanation: Germanium has a smaller band gap (about 0.7 eV) than silicon (about 1.1 eV), so at the same temperature many more electrons are thermally excited across the gap: A is true. R is also true, but both materials are elemental semiconductors, so being elemental cannot account for the difference between them. R is true but does not explain A.
steps: A: true (smaller E_g → more electron-hole pairs)
R: true (Ge and Si are both elemental)
R names a property the two share, so it cannot explain a difference → B
solution.why_others_wrong: The reason for A is the smaller band gap of germanium, not the fact that it is elemental, so 'R is the correct explanation' is wrong; both statements are true, so C and D are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', classification of metals, conductors and semiconductors; intrinsic semiconductor
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An alternating voltage v = 20 sin(100πt) volt (t in seconds) is applied to a half-wave rectifier consisting of an ideal diode in series with a load resistor. The peak voltage across the load and the frequency of the rectified output are:

solution.concept: Half-wave rectifier: one output pulse per input cycle; ideal diode → no voltage lost
solution.explanation: The input has peak value 20 V and ω = 100π rad/s, i.e. f = 50 Hz. An ideal diode passes the positive half cycles unchanged, so the output peaks at 20 V and repeats once per input cycle.
steps: Half-wave: output frequency = input frequency = 50 Hz
solution.why_others_wrong: 14.1 V is the rms value of the input, not the peak of the output. 100 Hz is the output frequency of a full-wave rectifier. 10 V halves the peak, but the diode removes half of each cycle, not half of the amplitude.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', application of junction diode as a rectifier

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Each solar cell of a certain type gives 0.50 V and 2.0 A at its operating point in sunlight. A panel is to supply 12 V and 6.0 A at the same operating point. Arranging the cells in identical series strings connected in parallel, the least number of cells needed is:

solution.concept: Cells in series add voltages; identical strings in parallel add currents
solution.explanation: Each string must give 12 V, so it needs 12/0.50 = 24 cells in series and carries 2.0 A. To deliver 6.0 A, three such strings are joined in parallel.
solution.why_others_wrong: 24 gives the right voltage but only 2.0 A. 27 adds the two numbers instead of multiplying. 3 gives the right current but only 0.50 V.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', optoelectronic junction devices (solar cell)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Silicon with an intrinsic carrier concentration of 1.0 × 10¹⁶ m⁻³ is doped with 1.0 × 10²² m⁻³ donor atoms, all of which are ionised. In thermal equilibrium, the ratio of the concentration of majority carriers to that of minority carriers is about:

solution.concept: n_e ≈ N_D for n-type; mass-action law n_e n_h = n_i²
solution.explanation: The donors supply n_e ≈ 10²² m⁻³ electrons (majority carriers). The hole concentration is then fixed by n_e n_h = n_i².
solution.why_others_wrong: 10⁶ compares the electrons with the intrinsic concentration instead of with the holes. 10²² is the electron concentration itself, not a ratio. 10⁻¹² inverts the ratio (minority to majority).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', extrinsic semiconductor

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): At absolute zero, n-type silicon conducts electricity well, because its donor atoms supply free electrons.
Reason (R): In n-type silicon, the donor energy level lies only a little (about 0.05 eV) below the bottom of the conduction band.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Ionisation of donors needs (a little) thermal energy
solution.explanation: R is true: NCERT shows the donor level just below the conduction band, about 0.05 eV for silicon. But even this small energy must come from thermal agitation; at 0 K there is none, so the donor electrons stay bound and no electrons are in the conduction band. The semiconductor behaves as an insulator at 0 K, so A is false.
steps: R: E_d ≈ 0.05 eV below E_c in Si → true
A: at 0 K no thermal energy → donors not ionised → insulator → false
solution.why_others_wrong: A is false, so options that take it as true are wrong; at room temperature (kT ≈ 0.026 eV) most donors are ionised, but not at 0 K.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', extrinsic semiconductor (energy band diagram)
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match each logic expression in List-I (inputs A and B) with the expression it is always equal to in List-II. (Check with truth tables if needed.)

List-I:
A. NOT (A + B), the output of a NOR gate
B. NOT (A · B), the output of a NAND gate
C. A + (A · B)
D. NOT ((NOT A) + (NOT B))

List-II:
I. A · B
II. (NOT A) + (NOT B)
III. (NOT A) · (NOT B)
IV. A

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Truth tables of OR, AND, NOT, NAND and NOR
solution.explanation: Write the outputs for (A, B) = (0, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (1, 1). NOR gives 1, 0, 0, 0, the same as (NOT A)·(NOT B). NAND gives 1, 1, 1, 0, the same as (NOT A) + (NOT B). A + A·B gives 0, 0, 1, 1, which is just A. NOT((NOT A) + (NOT B)) gives 0, 0, 0, 1, which is A·B.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes swap the NOR and NAND equivalents (the NOR output is 1 only for 0, 0; the NAND output is 0 only for 1, 1), or swap A + A·B (equal to A) with A·B.
solution.ncert_reference: NMC syllabus, logic gates (OR, AND, NOT, NAND and NOR)
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-III, B-II, C-IV, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
The secondary of a transformer gives 12 V (rms) at 50 Hz. It feeds a half-wave rectifier consisting of an ideal diode in series with a 1.0 kΩ load resistor. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) The peak current through the load is about 17 mA.
(b) The diode conducts during one half of each input cycle.
(c) The current pulses through the load occur at a frequency of 100 Hz.
(d) During the non-conducting half cycle, the reverse voltage across the diode reaches about 17 V.
(e) Doubling the load resistance doubles the frequency of the current pulses.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Half-wave rectification with an ideal diode; peak = √2 × rms
solution.explanation: The peak secondary voltage is 12√2 ≈ 17 V, so the peak load current is about 17 V/1.0 kΩ = 17 mA (a true). The diode conducts only when forward biased, i.e. during one half of each cycle (b true), so there is one pulse per cycle: 50 pulses per second, not 100 (c false). When the diode is off, no current flows and there is no drop across the load, so the full secondary voltage, up to about 17 V, appears across the diode (d true). The pulse frequency is set by the supply, not by the load (e false).
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (c) give the full-wave pulse frequency; options with (e) let the load change the frequency. The option without (a) misses the √2 relation between rms and peak values.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', application of junction diode as a rectifier

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Heavily doping both the p-side and the n-side of a p-n junction makes its depletion region thinner.
Statement II: Forward biasing a p-n junction decreases the diffusion current of majority carriers across it.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Depletion width and doping; effect of forward bias on the barrier
solution.explanation: With heavy doping, the charge needed to set up the barrier is found within a short distance of the junction, so the depletion region is very thin; NCERT uses this to explain the Zener diode (Statement I true). Forward bias lowers the potential barrier, so many more majority carriers can diffuse across: the diffusion current increases greatly (Statement II false).
steps: I: heavy doping → thin depletion layer (Zener diode) → true
II: lower barrier → more diffusion → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II reverses the effect of forward bias; it is under reverse bias that the diffusion current falls.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', p-n junction diode under forward bias; Zener diode
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A silicon crystal (intrinsic carrier concentration 1.5 × 10¹⁶ m⁻³) is doped with 1.0 × 10²¹ m⁻³ donor atoms and also with 1.0 × 10²¹ m⁻³ acceptor atoms, all of which are ionised. In thermal equilibrium, the electron and hole concentrations are:

options.text: both zero, because the electrons from the donors fill the acceptors

solution.concept: Charge neutrality n_e + N_A = n_h + N_D, together with n_e n_h = n_i²
solution.explanation: The electrons released by the donors are taken up by the equal number of acceptors, so the dopants compensate each other. Charge neutrality gives n_e = n_h, and the mass-action law then gives n_e = n_h = n_i: the crystal behaves like intrinsic silicon as far as carrier numbers are concerned.
steps: n_e n_h = n_i² → n_e = n_h = n_i = 1.5 × 10¹⁶ m⁻³
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.0 × 10²¹ m⁻³ for both ignores the recombination of donor electrons with acceptor holes. 2.0 × 10²¹ m⁻³ adds the two dopings as if both were donors. Zero ignores the thermally generated electron-hole pairs, which remain at the intrinsic level.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors (n_e n_h = n_i²)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A Zener diode of breakdown voltage 9.0 V is connected through a 300 Ω series resistor to a 15 V DC supply, and a 1.5 kΩ load resistor is connected across the Zener diode, which is in its breakdown region (take its voltage as constant). Match each quantity in List-I with its value in List-II.

List-I:
A. Current through the series resistor
B. Current through the load
C. Current through the Zener diode
D. Power dissipated in the series resistor

List-II:
I. 6.0 mA
II. 120 mW
III. 20 mA
IV. 14 mA

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Zener regulator: V_load = V_Z; I_series = (V_in − V_Z)/R_s; I_Z = I_series − I_load
solution.explanation: The Zener holds the load at 9.0 V. The series resistor drops the remaining 6.0 V and carries the total current, which divides between the load and the Zener.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes exchange the series and Zener currents (the Zener carries only what the load does not take), or the load current with the Zener current.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', Zener diode (as a voltage regulator)
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A 12 V DC supply is connected through a 100 Ω resistor to a Zener diode of breakdown voltage 5.0 V, which is in its breakdown region. Connected across the Zener diode is a branch consisting of an LED in series with a 150 Ω resistor; the LED has a constant forward voltage of 2.0 V when it conducts. The current through the Zener diode is:

solution.concept: Zener regulator feeding a load; LED forward drop in series with its resistor
solution.explanation: The Zener fixes 5.0 V across the LED branch. The LED takes 2.0 V, leaving 3.0 V across its 150 Ω resistor. The 100 Ω resistor drops 12 − 5.0 = 7.0 V and carries the total current, which divides between the LED branch and the Zener.
solution.why_others_wrong: 70 mA is the total current in the 100 Ω resistor. 20 mA is the LED current. 90 mA adds the two instead of subtracting.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', Zener diode (as a voltage regulator); light emitting diode

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Inputs A and B are fed both to a NOR gate (output X) and to an AND gate (output Y). X and Y are then fed to a second NOR gate, whose output is Z. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) Z = 0 when A = 0 and B = 0.
(b) Z = 1 when A = 1 and B = 0.
(c) Z = 1 when A = 1 and B = 1.
(d) Z = 1 when A = 0 and B = 1.
(e) If the second NOR gate is replaced by an OR gate, the new output is 1 only when A and B are equal.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Truth tables of NOR, AND and OR
solution.explanation: For (0, 0): X = 1, Y = 0, so Z = NOR(1, 0) = 0 (a true). For (1, 0) and (0, 1): X = 0, Y = 0, so Z = 1 (b, d true). For (1, 1): X = 0, Y = 1, so Z = 0 (c false). With an OR gate in place of the second NOR, the output is OR(X, Y): 1 for (0, 0) and (1, 1), 0 otherwise, i.e. 1 only when A = B (e true).
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (c) forget that the AND output Y = 1 for (1, 1) makes the final NOR output 0. Options leaving out (b) or (e) miss correct rows of the truth table.
solution.ncert_reference: NMC syllabus, logic gates (OR, AND, NOT, NAND and NOR)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A light-emitting diode is made of a semiconductor with a band gap of 1.9 eV. Take hc = 1240 eV nm. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) It emits red light of wavelength about 650 nm.
(b) It emits light only when it is forward biased.
(c) A photodiode made of the same semiconductor would respond to light of wavelength 500 nm.
(d) The light is emitted when electrons and holes recombine near the junction, the energy being released as photons.
(e) Increasing the forward current makes the LED emit light of a shorter wavelength.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: LED: photon energy ≈ band gap; photodiode responds when hν > E_g
solution.explanation: λ ≈ hc/E_g = 1240/1.9 ≈ 650 nm, red (a true). Under forward bias, electrons and holes are injected across the junction and recombine, releasing their energy as photons (b and d true). A photon of 500 nm carries 1240/500 ≈ 2.5 eV, more than 1.9 eV, so it can create electron-hole pairs in a photodiode of this material (c true). A larger forward current increases the intensity of the light, not its photon energy; the colour is fixed by the band gap (e false).
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (e) confuse brightness with colour. Options leaving out (c) forget that photons with more energy than the band gap are also absorbed.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', optoelectronic junction devices (photodiode, light emitting diode)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The depth of a small beaker is to be measured with a vernier calipers. The part of the instrument used for this is:

options.text: the lower (main) jaws, placed against the outside of the beaker
the upper jaws, placed against the inner walls of the beaker
the thin strip (depth rod) that slides out of the end of the main scale as the vernier is moved
the circular scale, turned until the rod touches the bottom

solution.concept: Parts of a vernier calipers and their uses
solution.explanation: A vernier calipers has three measuring parts: the lower jaws for external dimensions (outer diameter), the upper jaws for internal dimensions (inner diameter), and a thin strip attached to the vernier, which projects from the end of the main scale and is used to measure depth. The end of the main scale rests on the rim and the strip is pushed down until it touches the bottom.
steps: Outer size → lower jaws; inner size → upper jaws; depth → depth strip
solution.why_others_wrong: The lower jaws measure external dimensions and the upper jaws internal ones. A circular scale belongs to a screw gauge, not to a vernier calipers.
solution.ncert_reference: NCERT Physics laboratory work (NMC experimental skills), vernier calipers - internal and external diameter and depth of a vessel
solution.final_answer: Option C: the thin strip (depth rod) that slides out of the end of the main scale as the vernier is moved

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A copper calorimeter of mass 200 g is used in a method-of-mixtures experiment. Taking the specific heat capacity of copper as 420 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ and that of water as 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, the water equivalent of the calorimeter is:

solution.concept: Water equivalent W = m s/s_w: the mass of water with the same heat capacity
solution.explanation: The calorimeter absorbs as much heat per kelvin as a mass W of water, where W s_w = m s.
solution.why_others_wrong: 200 g is the actual mass of the calorimeter, not its water equivalent. 2.0 g and 2.0 kg are out by a factor of 10 or 100 in the arithmetic of the ratio 420/4200 = 1/10.
solution.ncert_reference: NCERT Physics laboratory work (NMC experimental skills), specific heat capacity by the method of mixtures

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: To reduce random error in measuring the diameter of a wire with a screw gauge, readings are taken at several places along the wire, in two mutually perpendicular directions at each place, and their mean is taken.
Statement II: The pitch of a screw gauge is the distance moved by its spindle (screw) in one complete rotation of the circular scale.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Use of the screw gauge; pitch and least count
solution.explanation: A wire may not be perfectly uniform or perfectly round, so readings at different places and in two perpendicular directions are averaged (Statement I true). The pitch is the linear distance advanced per full turn; dividing it by the number of circular-scale divisions gives the least count (Statement II true).
solution.why_others_wrong: Both are correct descriptions of the screw gauge experiment.
solution.ncert_reference: NCERT Physics laboratory work (NMC experimental skills), screw gauge - diameter of a given wire
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A vernier calipers has a least count of 0.01 cm, its vernier scale having 10 divisions. With the jaws closed, the zero of the vernier scale lies to the left of the zero of the main scale, and the 7th vernier division coincides with a main-scale division. While measuring the diameter of a rod, the main-scale reading is 3.2 cm and the 4th vernier division coincides. The corrected diameter of the rod is:

solution.concept: Negative zero error = −(N − n) × LC when the vernier zero is to the left; corrected reading = observed − zero error
solution.explanation: With the vernier zero to the left of the main-scale zero, the instrument reads too little: the zero error is negative. If the nth of N vernier divisions coincides, the zero error is −(N − n) × LC.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3.21 cm subtracts 0.03 cm, treating the error as positive. 3.17 cm and 3.31 cm take the zero error as −0.07 cm or +0.07 cm (7 × LC), as if it were read like a positive zero error.
solution.ncert_reference: NCERT Physics laboratory work (NMC experimental skills), vernier calipers (zero error and zero correction)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In a simple pendulum experiment, the length of the string is measured from the point of suspension to the hook of the bob, the radius of the bob being unknown. With a string length of 101 cm the time period is 2.0 s, and with a string length of 26 cm it is 1.0 s. The value of g obtained from these readings is about:

solution.concept: T = 2π√(L_eff/g), with L_eff = L + x, where x (the unknown hook-to-centre distance) is the same in both readings
solution.explanation: Write T² = (4π²/g)(L + x) for both lengths and subtract: the unknown x cancels, leaving g = 4π²(L₁ − L₂)/(T₁² − T₂²).
solution.why_others_wrong: 9.97 m/s² and 10.3 m/s² use one reading alone, ignoring the unknown distance from the hook to the centre of the bob. 7.40 m/s² divides by T₁² instead of by T₁² − T₂².
solution.ncert_reference: NCERT Physics laboratory work (NMC experimental skills), simple pendulum (time period and effective length)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In a metre bridge experiment with a 6.0 Ω standard resistance in the right gap, the null point is 40.0 cm from the left end when a resistor X₁ is in the left gap, and 50.0 cm from the left end when a resistor X₂ is in the left gap instead. When X₁ and X₂ are connected in series in the left gap, the null point is expected at:

solution.concept: Metre bridge balance X/R = l/(100 − l); resistors in series add
solution.explanation: Find X₁ and X₂ from the first two balance points, add them for the series combination, and use the balance condition again to locate the new null point.
solution.why_others_wrong: 90.0 cm adds the two balancing lengths, but it is the resistances, not the lengths, that add. 45.0 cm averages the lengths. 37.5 cm is measured from the wrong end (100 − 62.5).
solution.ncert_reference: NCERT Physics laboratory work (NMC experimental skills), metre bridge - verification of the laws of combination (series) of resistances

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match each measuring instrument in List-I with its least count in List-II.

List-I:
A. Vernier calipers in which 10 vernier divisions equal 9 main-scale divisions of 1 mm
B. Screw gauge of pitch 0.5 mm with 50 divisions on its circular scale
C. Screw gauge of pitch 1 mm with 50 divisions on its circular scale
D. Vernier calipers in which 20 vernier divisions equal 19 main-scale divisions of 1 mm

List-II:
I. 0.01 mm
II. 0.05 mm
III. 0.1 mm
IV. 0.02 mm

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Vernier: LC = 1 MSD − 1 VSD; screw gauge: LC = pitch/number of circular-scale divisions
solution.explanation: For a vernier, N VSD = (N − 1) MSD gives LC = MSD/N. For a screw gauge, LC = pitch divided by the number of circular-scale divisions.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes exchange the two verniers (0.1 mm and 0.05 mm) or the two screw gauges (0.01 mm and 0.02 mm), which differ in N or in the pitch.
solution.ncert_reference: NCERT Physics laboratory work (NMC experimental skills), vernier calipers and screw gauge (least count)
solution.final_answer: Option A: A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: While drawing the reverse-bias characteristic of a Zener diode, a student finds that in the breakdown region the reverse voltage across the diode is 6.20 V when the reverse current is 10 mA, and 6.25 V when the current is 20 mA. The resistance of the Zener diode in this region, found from the slope of the characteristic, is:

solution.concept: Dynamic resistance r = ΔV/ΔI from the characteristic curve
solution.explanation: In the breakdown region the voltage hardly changes while the current changes a lot; the dynamic resistance is the ratio of the small change in voltage to the change in current. Its small value is why the Zener diode regulates voltage well.
solution.why_others_wrong: 620 Ω and 312 Ω are the static ratios V/I at the two points, not the slope. 0.20 Ω inverts the ratio (ΔI/ΔV in A/V, i.e. a conductance in siemens).
solution.ncert_reference: NCERT Physics laboratory work (NMC experimental skills), characteristic curves of a Zener diode and its reverse breakdown voltage

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In the capillary-rise experiment, pure water rises 3.0 cm in a clean glass capillary tube of internal radius 0.50 mm. A detergent solution, whose density may be taken equal to that of water, rises 2.0 cm in another clean capillary of internal radius 0.40 mm. Taking the angle of contact as zero in both cases, the ratio of the surface tension of the detergent solution to that of pure water is:

solution.concept: Capillary rise h = 2T/(rρg) for zero angle of contact, so T ∝ hr (same density)
solution.explanation: The detergent lowers the surface tension of water, which is the effect this experiment shows. Because the two tubes are different, both the height and the radius must be used: T = rhρg/2.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2/3 compares the heights alone, ignoring the different radii. 5/6 multiplies the height ratio by r₁/r₂ instead of r₂/r₁ (as if h were proportional to r). 15/8 inverts the ratio; the detergent lowers the surface tension.
solution.ncert_reference: NCERT Physics laboratory work (NMC experimental skills), surface tension of water by capillary rise and effect of detergents

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
In the experiment to find the coefficient of viscosity of a liquid from the terminal velocity of a falling steel ball, which of the following statements are correct?

(a) The ball reaches its terminal velocity when its weight is balanced by the upthrust and the viscous drag together.
(b) For balls of the same material falling through the same liquid, the terminal velocity is proportional to the square of the radius.
(c) The ball should be dropped close to the wall of the jar so that its fall can be watched clearly.
(d) If the temperature of the liquid rises, the terminal velocity of a given ball increases, because the viscosity of a liquid decreases with temperature.
(e) The terminal velocity does not depend on the density of the liquid.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Stokes' law: at terminal velocity (4/3)πr³(ρ − σ)g = 6πηrv, so v = 2r²(ρ − σ)g/(9η)
solution.explanation: At terminal velocity there is no acceleration: weight = upthrust + viscous force (a true). This gives v = 2r²(ρ − σ)g/(9η), so v ∝ r² for the same materials (b true) and v depends on the liquid's density σ (e false). The viscosity of liquids decreases as their temperature rises, so v increases (d true). Stokes' law holds for a ball moving through a liquid extending far on all sides, so the ball is dropped along the axis, away from the walls (c false).
steps: (c) the walls disturb the flow → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (c) contradict the precaution of keeping the ball away from the walls; options with (e) forget the upthrust term (ρ − σ).
solution.ncert_reference: NCERT Physics laboratory work (NMC experimental skills), coefficient of viscosity by terminal velocity; Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Fluids', viscosity
